title: Replicable science depends on simplicity and speed
text:
Replicable science depends on simplicity and speed
2025-07-29
If replicating a project requires almost as much time as the doing original research, it is barely replication. Speed compression fully defines how valuable the science is. But what does that look like currently? Below I have a single screenshot of something pretty darn close to the “gold standard” of replicability. All the researcher told me was the “look it up on my github.” The full process to replicate is then pictured below.

This produced identical CSVs to what the researcher claimed their research did. Total time from hearing about the github repository to fully replicating their result: about 30 seconds. THAT is replicable science.
To showcase the simplicity exhibited here, there were only 3 real steps, highlighed below.


I used git to get the full history of the code and cloned it onto my computer. In this case, the repository also included the data, which worked because the data were pretty small. Sometimes the data step is really hard if the data are too big to fit in git (less than 5mb or so).
I used Anaconda (specifically miniforge3) to install python and get the hundreds of open-source libraries a modern data scientist uses. This command simply activates that environment I already set up. On possible improvement to this repository would be to include the method for creating the environment itself (by including an environment.yml file which tells Anaconda what to install). Environment management is a very common time-sink/challenge, but it’s getting easier. Check out our devstack installation steps for more info.
I called the python command and pointed it to the run_renewable_energy_production.py file. Identifying the correct python file to run varies from project to project, but a good repo will have a readme.md file displayed at its root that give a “quickstart” explanation defining this file.

In this wild west of AI, we need to ask “what does it even mean to be a good researcher”, or even “what does it mean to be true”. Effective replicability, in my opinion, is the best candidate to answer both of these.

title: Installing the GTAP toolchain
text:
GTAPpy is a thin Python layer over a stack of Windows programs from Purdue and CoPS. Installing GTAPpy itself is the easy part; the work is getting that stack in place and licensed. There are four pieces, and they have to be installed in roughly this order:








piece
what it is
why you need it




Microsoft C++ Build Tools
MSVC compiler
builds the Cython extensions in Hazelbean, which GTAPpy imports


GEMPACK (gpei)
the CGE solver
actually solves the GTAP model


RunGTAP
GUI front end
ships the compiled v7 model code and is how you produce a working version directory


GTAPAgg2
database aggregator
turns the licensed GTAP database into the aggregation you want to run



GEMPACK, RunGTAP and GTAPAgg2 are Windows-only. On a Mac or Linux workstation the usual arrangement is a Windows VM holding the toolchain, driven over SSH — gtappy_runner.py has a run_gtap_cmf_on_vm path and a mac_to_win path translator for exactly this.


This step is not about GTAP at all. Hazelbean, which GTAPpy depends on, contains Cython extension modules, and pip has to compile them on install. On Windows that requires the MSVC compiler, and the error you get without it (“Microsoft Visual C++ 14.0 or greater is required”) is the most common first-run failure in the whole devstack.
The Python packaging documentation’s Windows compilers page is the authority on which compiler version pairs with which Python. It is worth checking rather than guessing, because the requirement moves with each CPython release:



The Windows compilers page: which MSVC version current CPython is built with


The same page is where the “you only need this if you are compiling a Cython or Pyrex file” caveat comes from — which is precisely our case:



Compiling a Cython extension is what pulls in the compiler requirement


You do not need full Visual Studio. The standalone Build Tools for Visual Studio package is enough, and is a much smaller install:



The Build Tools for Visual Studio download page


If the current build tools do not match the compiler version your Python needs, older releases are reachable from the same site under “Still want an older version?”, though this requires a (free) Dev Essentials account:



Older Visual Studio releases, if you need a specific MSVC version


In the installer, the simple route is the Desktop development with C++ workload, which pulls in the compiler, the CRT and the Windows SDK together:



Selecting the Desktop development with C++ workload


If you would rather keep the install small, skip the workload and pick the components directly on the Individual components tab — the MSVC v143 x64/x86 build tools, the C++ build tools core features, the Windows Universal C Runtime, and a Windows SDK. That is roughly 100 MB more rather than the workload’s several GB:



Picking the individual components instead of the whole workload


Verify by opening a fresh shell and importing Hazelbean, which triggers compilation on first import:
import hazelbean as hb



GEMPACK is the solver. Download the executable-image release from CoPS at https://www.copsmodels.com/gpeidl.htm — for example gpei-12.1.004-install.exe (or the 12.0 build if you need to match an older model release).
Install to the default location. GEMPACK expects to live at a short path with no spaces, and a lot of downstream configuration assumes C:\GP:



GEMPACK installs to C:\GP by default — keep it


Proceed without selecting a licence file. That starts the six-month trial, which is enough to get a working setup before a licence is sorted out.
The path you install to is the one GTAPpy needs to know about; in a run file it is set as the GEMPACK utilities directory (historically p.gempack_utils_dir).



Install RunGTAP from https://www.gtap.agecon.purdue.edu/products/rungtap/default.asp.
RunGTAP is a GUI, and GTAPpy exists so you do not have to use it for production runs. You still need it installed, for two reasons: it ships with a compiled copy of the GTAP v7 model code, which is where the version directory GTAPpy runs against ultimately comes from; and it is the most convenient place to sanity-check a new database or a new shock before wiring it into a task tree. Both of those are covered in Running GTAP by hand.









ImportantThis step needs a GTAP database licence



Everything below requires access to the GTAP database, which is licensed from Purdue. Within our group you can instead reach an already-licensed copy through the ee_internal database — use hb.get_path() against the private bucket rather than downloading and aggregating yourself. The manual route is documented here because someone has to do it once per database release, and because it explains where the files GTAPpy consumes come from.


Get GTAPAgg2 from https://www.gtap.agecon.purdue.edu/private/secured.asp?Sec_ID=1055.
Get the licence file. Step 2 of https://www.gtap.agecon.purdue.edu/databases/download.asp yields a .lic file. Put it in the GTAPAgg2 directory — the aggregator reads it from there and the title bar shows the licence it found.
Get the database itself, from the same download page. Take the standard package and the AEZ (Land Use and Cover) version — the AEZ extension is what carries land by agro-ecological zone, which is the whole point of the land-use work the devstack does with GTAP:



Download the GTAP Land Use and Cover Data Base alongside the standard package


Each download is a .pkg file; put both in the GTAPAgg2 directory. When you launch GTAPAgg2, point it at both packages so the AEZ product is selectable under Choose source data. Getting this wrong is a quiet failure — you get a perfectly valid database that simply has no AEZ detail in it:



Choose source data: pick GTAP-AEZ, not plain GTAP, when you want land by AEZ


With the toolchain installed, continue to Building an aggregated database.

title: Contributing to Devstack’s Base Data
text:
Our base data is becoming a valuable asset that accelerates our shared work. Towards that, this page documents how you could contribute (if you want) your project’s data so that it works seamlessly with the rest of the devstack. When done correctly, our base_data has two useful aspects:

Files are automatically downloaded by the get_path() function.
All rasters are Pyramidal Cloud Optimized Geotiffs (POGs), which enables, among many other things

The ability to download a subset of a single raster
The ability to use precise and very fast zonal statistics
Very accurate area-per-cell calculations (without imprecision from using projected data)




To make one’s project fully replicable, it obviously needs to have an open git repo for the code. The challenge, though, is that git is not good for managing data, so if someone clones your code, it will probably fail because it doesn’t (and shouldn’t if the data is > 5MB) include the data in the repo. The way our Devstack manages base_data is that it is automatically downloaded via p.get_path() when it is needed. Thus, if you want your project to “just work”, we need to figure out how to create a good system for proposing new contributions to the base data and then cleaning/curating them so they work well. 



The above only works if your data is included in our base_data in the proper location and in the proper format. Here we discuss how you can contribute it into the base data so your code works for everyone else (in the lab, and optionally for the general public).

Move your data into our TEEMs drive in the base_data submissions folder in a single folder with your project’s name. See the example below for the full base_data location and a few example projects.



Change your git repo so that that ALL (ABSOLUTELY ALL) data are referenced via a relative path into this submissions base_data folder. So, for instance, if you had a file “emissions_factors.csv” in the air_quality project, the code would reference it as

data_ref_path = os.path.join("submissions", "air_quality", "emissions_factors.csv"
The data_ref_path is what we call a Reference Path (or Ref Path), which get_path(data_ref_path) can find and download; the canonical definition, including the full order of directories get_path searches, is in Conventions.

Put a Readme.md in your submission folder. It should reference the code used to produce it and basic information on units, interpretation, and how it should be used.
After you complete 1-3, email me! I will then test your repo and code by cloning the repo, modifying ONLY the base_data_dir, and then check that everything runs.
I will then further clean the data (to be compliant with the conventions defined here https://justinandrewjohnson.com/earth_economy_devstack/conventions.html, and specifically, to be a POG. I’m happy to do the cleaning, but if you want, you might want to consider following the conventions earlier in your project rather than later. 
I’ll write “unittests” that ensure your code and data work, which will be automatically run when there’s a new release of the devstack repo.
If everything passes, the data get “promoted” to base_data by eliminating the word “submissions” in their file path (e.g., base_data\submissions\emissions_factors.csv becomes base_data\emissions_factors.csv)

If all these edits are done, you can now change your code to use the Reference Path and it will work for you and for everybody else too.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text: Local climate regulation is urban cooling. Vegetation lowers city temperatures, buildings spend less electricity on air conditioning, and the account values that saved electricity. The base year is 2019 and the price convention recorded in es_config.csv is avoided energy cost.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Quantity
InVEST urban cooling gives each city-month a vegetation cooling effect, which the calculation converts into an electricity difference in kilowatt-hours, the kwh_diff column of the committed city-month files.
The cooling-degree measure behind that conversion is temp_degc_to_cdd_smooth, v04’s smoothed exceedance. Below the base minus the window it returns zero, above the base plus the window it is linear in temperature, and across the window it follows smoothstep01, the cubic \(t^2(3-2t)\) on [0, 1].

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Price
The national electricity price in USD per kilowatt-hour, the price_usd_per_kwh column.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Valuation
\[
\text{total\_savings\_usd} = \text{kwh\_diff} \times \text{price\_usd\_per\_kwh}
\]
city_savings_identity recomputes that product at rtol 1e-6 and raises if it breaks. Summing cities to countries gives the December 2025 version of the accounting table.
The current final applies v04’s correction, written explicitly in that version’s code and ported verbatim in apply_country_marginal_consumption. It divides out the old global marginal-consumption slope embedded in the v02 values and multiplies by each country’s own consumption per cooling-degree-day, which is cooling energy per capita over the IEA-CMCC 2019 humid-CDD total.
\[
\text{corrected} = \frac{\text{value}}{\text{URBAN\_COOLING\_OLD\_GLOBAL\_MC}} \times \text{consumption per CDD}
\]

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
What the library reports
gep_calculation reads the committed final table, parses its dollar-formatted string column through parse_dollar_column, and joins it onto the r250 country list by label.
Three things verify against staged data. The kilowatt-hour times price identity is exact. The merged-sum identity against the December 2025 version is exact on every country tested. The current final’s parse and totals check out.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the local_climate_regulation service:

local_climate_regulation_final_path, the committed final accounting table.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Output
gep_calculation writes gep_by_country_base_year.csv into its own task directory, holding the r250 identifiers and attributes, year, and local_climate_regulation_gep.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Method constants

URBAN_COOLING_OLD_GLOBAL_MC = 1.71737465916468, the old global marginal-consumption slope that v04 divides out.
URBAN_COOLING_CDD_BASE_C = 18.0, the humid cooling-degree-day base the calculation uses (CDDhum18).
URBAN_COOLING_SMOOTH_WINDOW_C = 1.0, the width of the smoothing window either side of the base.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Taken as given
The InVEST urban cooling run itself and the national electricity prices.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
What is open
The v04 correction’s own inputs are not reproducible here. The IEA-CMCC cooling-degree-day file and the v2_nkd energy workbook live only on the author’s machine, and the staged VERSION4 energy CSV is a different vintage that does not validate the inversion. Those two files are the named asks.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Terrestrial Carbon Storage
text: This section outlines how we value carbon sequestration as an ecosystem service within the GEP framework. The analysis focuses specifically on carbon sequestration provided by terrestrial ecosystems, which is appraised in terms of its contribution to climate change mitigation. By quantifying the carbon sequestration capacity of these ecosystems, we aim to capture their role in reducing atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations, thereby contributing to global climate regulation.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Terrestrial Carbon Storage
text:
Estimating Quantity
We followed the methodology outlined in Johnson et al. (2023) to quantify global carbon sequestration. To estimate the quantity of carbon sequestered, we implemented a two-stage modeling framework, as illustrated in panels (a) and (b) of Figure 1.
First, we utilized an advanced global carbon density map developed by Spawn et al. (2020) to update the carbon pool. This dataset consists of harmonized vegetation-specific maps that integrate both aboveground and belowground biomass into a single, comprehensive spatial representation for the year 2010, thereby enabling more accurate assessments of carbon stocks across diverse ecosystems. To construct the carbon pool table or carbon density lookup table, we combined the 300 m land use and land cover (LULC) data from the European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative Land Cover (ESA CCI LC) with the carbon zone map employed by Ruesch and Gibbs (2008). This integrated methodology enhances both the spatial resolution and contextual relevance of carbon stock estimations.
Second, we applied the updated carbon density lookup table and the carbon zone map to a time series of LULC data, also derived from ESA CCI LC, to enable dynamic assessments of carbon storage over time.






Figure 1: Workflow for quantifying and valuing global carbon storage. (a) The Data Preparation phase integrates the carbon zone map employed by Ruesch and Gibbs (2008), base-year ESA LULC data, and carbon density data from Spawn et al. (2020) to generate a carbon density lookup table. (b) The Application phase applies the lookup table to the base-year LULC and carbon zone maps to obtain per-cell carbon density, then multiplies by cell area to obtain per-cell carbon stocks. The same calculation applies to any LULC time series for dynamic assessment. (c) The Valuation phase sums carbon stocks per country and multiplies by the annual rental social cost of carbon to yield GEP by country.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Terrestrial Carbon Storage
text:
Estimating Price
To estimate the value of carbon sequestration, we employed the rental social cost of carbon (SCC) (Parisa et al. 2022) as the pricing metric. Parisa et al. (2022) provides the theoretical rationale for quantifying the value of short-term carbon storage, which corresponds to carbon sequestration. Following this approach, and within the framework of Gross Ecosystem Product (GEP), we estimate the annual value of carbon sequestration as follows:
\[
\text{Carbon Rental Rate} = P_C(t) - P_C(t+1)e^{-r} = P_C(t)\left(1 - e^{-r} \right)
\]
where \(P_C(t)\) denotes the social cost of carbon in year \(t\), and \(r\) represents the net discount rate equal to the difference between the discount rate and the rate of growth of carbon prices. This formulation reflects the rental valuation approach, capturing the annualized benefit of temporarily storing one metric ton of CO2 for one year. This measure represents the annualized marginal damage cost of emitting an additional metric ton of CO2, thereby aligning our valuation approach with established climate policy frameworks and principles of intertemporal cost-benefit analysis. We adopt a carbon price of $678.33 per metric ton of carbon (C), corresponding to the mean social cost of CO2 of roughly $185 per metric ton of CO2 estimated by Rennert et al. (2022) (converted to a per-carbon basis by the 44/12 mass ratio). This value is employed for \(P_C(t)\), the carbon price at time \(t\), and a discount rate of 2% is applied, following the same source. The rental rate the model applies is read year by year from the carbon-price series (rental scc r2% in carbon_prices.xlsx); for the base year 2019 it is approximately $13.19 per ton of C. A flat 2% rate applied directly to $678.33 would give $13.43; the difference reflects the net discount rate \(r\) defined above, which nets out the growth in carbon prices.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Terrestrial Carbon Storage
text:
Valuation
After estimating both the quantity and price of carbon sequestration, the economic value of carbon sequestration, is calculated as:
\[
\text{GEP}_{\text{carbon storage and sequestration}} = Q \cdot P \cdot \lambda = \text{Carbon Storage} \times \text{Rental SCC} \times 1
\]
where \(Q\) represents the quantity of carbon storage (in metric tons), and \(P\) denotes the annual rental SCC per ton. This formulation aligns with the GEP framework, translating biophysical carbon sequestration into monetary value.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text: Extractive energy provision covers natural gas, coal and petroleum. The account values it as the resource rent each country earns from extraction, read from the World Bank’s Changing Wealth of Nations 2024 package at the GEP base year of 2019.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
Quantity and price
There is no separate quantity step and no separate price step. CWoN reports the rent itself, in current USD per country per year, so the module reads that number and carries it through. The price convention recorded for this service in es_config.csv is resource rent.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
Valuation
fuel_rent_by_country_from_cwon takes one CWoN table and returns one row per country holding the YR<year> column at the requested year. The CWoN tables are wide, keyed on countrycode with World Bank codes that match iso3_r250_label directly, Kosovo included as XKX.
extractive_energy_gep_from_cwon runs that read once per fuel and sums the three components with min_count=1. A country absent from one fuel’s table stays NaN in that component and still receives a service total from the components that do exist, so a country with only coal is a coal country rather than a missing one. Components sum by the same commodity convention that extractive materials provision uses.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, all scoped to the extractive_energy service:

extractive_energy_cwon_gas_path, extractive_energy_cwon_coal_path and extractive_energy_cwon_oil_path, the Stata rent tables the valuation computes from. Each carries a _source_url row pointing at the World Bank reproducibility archive and a _source_archive_member row naming the file inside it, under Reproducibility package/Output/Latest/.
extractive_energy_gas_path, extractive_energy_coal_path and extractive_energy_oil_path, the three committed per-country CSVs from the consortium drive, kept as the replication anchor.

The shared country references come from initialize_country_paths, which publishes the r264 correspondence and loads p.df_countries.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
Output
gep_calculation writes gep_by_country_base_year.csv into its own task directory. The columns are the r250 identifiers and attributes, year, the three per-fuel columns extractive_energy_gas_gep, extractive_energy_coal_gep and extractive_energy_oil_gep, and their sum extractive_energy_gep.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
Method constants
EXTRACTIVE_ENERGY_FUELS = ('gas', 'coal', 'oil') names the three components and fixes the order the summation reads them in.
COMMITTED_DUPLICATE_VALUE_ROWS records eight rows of the committed drive CSVs that carry another country’s full rent value. Bouvet Island and Svalbard take Norway’s, Christmas Island and the Cocos Islands take Australia’s, Tokelau takes New Zealand’s, Western Sahara takes Morocco’s, Palestine takes Israel’s, and Kosovo takes Serbia’s. In the Kosovo row the committed name column itself reads “Serbia”. The values were verified equal in every fuel where the row is non-empty.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
Taken as given
The CWoN rent estimation is upstream science and is used as published.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
What is open
The eight duplicate rows are a name-join artefact that counts the source countries twice, and for Kosovo it overrides the CWoN table’s own coal value. CWoN carries no rows at all for the first six. The module therefore computes from the CWoN tables, one country one row, rather than adopting the committed CSVs. gep_calculation logs the computed total beside the committed total so the gap stays visible on every run.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text: Water supply is built one component at a time. Hydropower direct use is complete and is what water_supply_gep currently carries. A water-use calculation covering agriculture, industry and municipal withdrawals is ported and reported beside it as separate columns. The price convention recorded in es_config.csv is resource rent (CWoN 2024), and the base year is 2019.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
Hydropower

Quantity and price
The hydropower valuation has no separate quantity and price step. CWoN 2024 publishes a capitalised hydropower wealth per country, and the annual rent that wealth implies is what the account wants.


Valuation
annuity_factor is the present value of one dollar a year over the CWoN horizon,
\[
A = \sum_{t=1}^{100} \frac{1}{(1+r)^t}, \qquad r = 0.04
\]
and hydropower_rent_from_wealth divides each country’s YR2019 wealth by it. Countries without wealth stay NaN, because no data is not zero rent.
The method was identified by reverse-engineering against the drive’s committed 2019 output, whose script is not on the drive. It is exact across all 94 valued countries, with the ratio constant to 1e-10. The test suite asserts the annuity identity and the exact replication. An earlier direct-use script on the drive, price times quantity from EIA and World Bank series dated November 2024, is superseded by this method and is not ported.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
Water use

Quantity and price
Withdrawal volumes in cubic metres per sector come from the withdrawal table. The price is the AQUASTAT SDG 6.4.1 water-use efficiency series in US dollars per cubic metre, one series per sector.


Valuation
clean_aquastat_water_efficiency is script 01 of the drive’s R calculation. It keeps the US$/m3 rows of the four SDG 6.4.1 series and pivots them wide by country and year.
water_use_gep_by_country_year is script 02. It applies three country renames onto the withdrawal table’s spellings, fills iso codes for the names its country map does not carry, drops the regional aggregate rows, merges the two tables, restricts to the survey years, and multiplies efficiency by withdrawal per sector to give gep_water_agricultural, gep_water_industrial and gep_water_municipal.
water_use_components_from_chain takes the latest survey year per country and keys it to r250 by exact country-name match, first on iso3_r250_name and then on name_long. A calculation country with no match keeps an empty iso3, so a name drift is visible instead of dropped.
Both of the R calculation’s own outputs replicate. The cleaned efficiency table matches bit-exactly. The country-year GEP table matches to the anchor CSV’s own 15-significant-digit rounding, maximum relative difference 3e-15.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the water_supply service:

water_supply_cwon_hydro_wealth_path, the CWoN hydro_wealth_cd table, with a _source_url row for the World Bank reproducibility archive and a _source_archive_member row naming the file inside it.
water_use_efficiency_input_path, the raw AQUASTAT export, with a _source_url row for the AQUASTAT data API.
water_use_withdrawal_path, the withdrawal table.
water_use_agriculture_path and water_use_all_sector_path, the drive’s committed per-country tables, held as comparison anchors.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
Outputs

hydropower_rent.csv from the hydropower_rent task.
aquastat_water_efficiency_cleaned.csv, water_use_gep_by_country_year.csv and water_use_components.csv from the water_use_components task.
gep_by_country_base_year.csv from gep_calculation, holding the r250 identifiers and attributes, year, hydropower_gep, water_use_agriculture_gep, water_use_all_sector_gep and water_supply_gep.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
Method constants

HYDROPOWER_DISCOUNT_RATE = 0.04, the CWoN standard discount.
HYDROPOWER_HORIZON_YEARS = 100, the CWoN capitalisation horizon.
HYDROPOWER_GEP_YEAR = 2019, the wealth column the rent is read from. Current USD equals real 2019 USD in the 2019 base year, and this is the only variant that covers Venezuela.
HYDROPOWER_REFERENCE_EXCLUDED, seventeen iso3 codes set to NaN to reproduce the reference: AZE, BGR, DOM, GRC, GTM, HTI, KAZ, LBR, MAR, MKD, NIC, POL, PRT, SLV, TJK, UKR and ZAF.
WATER_USE_YEARS = (2000, 2005, 2010, 2015), the AQUASTAT survey years the calculation keeps.
WATER_USE_EFFICIENCY_SERIES, WATER_USE_COUNTRY_RENAMES, WATER_USE_ISO_LOOKUP and WATER_USE_REGIONS_DROPPED, which reproduce script 02’s name surgery verbatim.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
Taken as given
CWoN’s own hydropower wealth estimate, and the AQUASTAT efficiency and withdrawal series.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
What is open
The seventeen excluded countries are the largest open item. The reference output leaves them empty although the CWoN wealth table values them, and no available material explains the drop, because the 2026 script is not on the drive and the package lacks its raw workbook. The exclusion is encoded to reproduce the reference, the reason is an ask on the deck, and changing the list is a reviewed-commit decision.
The drive’s per-country water-use tables are not this calculation’s outputs and are held as anchors rather than adopted. The agriculture table equals 1000 times GEP_total from a separate crop-water valuation whose scripts are not on the drive. The all-sector table was computed on a newer AQUASTAT vintage with the appendix’s deflate-to-2015 step, and only 3 of 183 countries reproduce from the staged inputs, with a median committed to computed-at-2019 ratio of 0.36 over a range of 0 to 1.25.
Script 02’s lookup countries keep their AQUASTAT names, so their efficiency and withdrawal rows share an iso code but never a country name. The merge leaves them as half-rows with no products, including USA, RUS and TUR. The anchor commits that behaviour and the port reproduces it.
water_supply_gep stays the hydropower component alone. How, and whether, the water-use components combine with it is the account’s subgroup question, flagged on the deck. The agriculture and household components named on the group’s sheet are not yet built anywhere we have seen, and the module is laid out to receive them beside hydropower.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text: Stormwater retention values the runoff that land cover holds back instead of sending into drainage systems. The account prices that volume at what it would cost to replace the same capacity. The base year is 2019 and the price convention recorded in es_config.csv is replacement cost.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
Quantity
Annual retained volume in cubic metres per country, from an InVEST Urban Stormwater Retention run over the inputs the consortium drive staged, the biophysical coefficient table, ESA 2020 land cover, WorldClim precipitation and SLGWRB soils. That run is made outside the task tree, on the drive’s own configuration, which base_data/global_invest/stormwater/run_recipe.md records. The retention_by_country task then sums the run’s retention raster inside each r250 country and writes the per-country table. The library reads that table; it does not run the retention model.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
Price
USD per cubic metre retained. The committed InVEST configuration prices retention at 1, which is a placeholder rather than a valuation. The intended price is the open ask, and it is held in one named constant until the author answers.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
Valuation
stormwater_gep_by_country is the whole valuation:
\[
\text{stormwater GEP} = \text{retention (m}^3) \times \text{price (USD/m}^3)
\]
The function is in place and unit-tested.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the stormwater service:

stormwater_retention_by_country_path, the per-country retention volumes the valuation prices.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
Output
gep_calculation writes gep_by_country_base_year.csv into its own task directory, holding iso3_r250_label, retention_m3, year and stormwater_gep. The log line reports the total retention in cubic metres a year, the number of countries with positive retention, the resulting GEP, and the placeholder price it was computed at.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
Method constants
STORMWATER_PRICE_PER_M3_PLACEHOLDER = 1.0, the committed configuration’s price per cubic metre.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
What is open
The price. Every output built on the placeholder is provisional by construction, which is why the constant is named for what it is and logged on every run. Whether the retained volumes should be masked to urban areas is the other open question. The run was made wall to wall over the global land cover, because the committed configuration carries no urban boundaries.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Value the deaths that forest root cohesion averts by holding hillslopes together. The service is computed as a difference between two runs of the same model on the same grid: one in which forest roots reinforce the soil as the land-cover map says they do, and one in which root cohesion is removed entirely. Everything else – terrain, soil, rainfall, population, roads, and the fitted statistical models – is identical between the two, so the difference in predicted deaths is attributable to root reinforcement alone.
This note describes what the code in global_invest/landslide_mitigation/ does. The science is a fold of m-braaksma/landslide_mitigation v0.2.0 (folded 2026-08-16); the arithmetic lives in landslide_mitigation_chain.py as pure functions, the raster drivers in landslide_mitigation_functions.py, and the pipeline in landslide_mitigation_tasks.py.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Value the deaths that forest root cohesion averts by holding hillslopes together. The service is computed as a difference between two runs of the same model on the same grid: one in which forest roots reinforce the soil as the land-cover map says they do, and one in which root cohesion is removed entirely. Everything else – terrain, soil, rainfall, population, roads, and the fitted statistical models – is identical between the two, so the difference in predicted deaths is attributable to root reinforcement alone.
This note describes what the code in global_invest/landslide_mitigation/ does. The science is a fold of m-braaksma/landslide_mitigation v0.2.0 (folded 2026-08-16); the arithmetic lives in landslide_mitigation_chain.py as pure functions, the raster drivers in landslide_mitigation_functions.py, and the pipeline in landslide_mitigation_tasks.py.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Grid and inputs
Everything is computed on the NSIDC EASE-Grid 2.0 global 1km grid (EPSG:6933), built from the authoritative EASE2_M01km.gpd grid definition rather than assumed. EASE-Grid is equal-area, so a pixel count converts to real area by one constant multiply and no latitude weighting is needed anywhere in the calculation. Every input is warped onto that exact grid and then checked against it for matching size, pixel resolution and projection before the model runs.








Input
Source
Resampling onto the 1km grid




Elevation
SEALS alt_m.tif (shared base data)
average


Agro-ecological zones
FAO GAEZ v5 AEZ57
mode (categorical)


Forest cover

class weights, then average


Landslide events

coordinate transform, not a warp


Population
LandScan, per year
sum (conserves counts)


Soil texture, organic carbon, bulk density
SoilGrids 0-5, 5-15, 15-30cm
thickness-weighted mean, then average


Saturated conductivity
HiHydroSoil 0-5, 5-15, 15-30cm
thickness-weighted mean, then average


Soil and sediment thickness

average


Mean annual precipitation
WorldClim BIO12 (1970-2000 normal)
average


Annual maximum daily rainfall
ERA5-Land, per year
bilinear (upsampling)


Road density
GRIP4 total density, m/km²
bilinear (upsampling)



The three soil-depth intervals are combined by their own thickness (5, 10 and 15cm), and only where each interval has data, so a pixel missing the deepest layer is the mean of the two shallower ones rather than a hole.
Forest cover enters as a root-reinforcement weight, not as a binary forest mask. Closed-canopy and flooded tree-cover classes take weight 1; the two mosaic tree/shrub-herbaceous classes are 50/50 land cover and take 0.5; sparse tree cover below 15% takes 0, as being below meaningful root reinforcement. Every other class is 0. Averaging that 0-1 weight field onto the 1km grid gives each pixel a fractional forest share.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Slope
Slope is computed with gdal.DEMProcessing (Horn 1981) from the raw elevation at four times the target resolution (~250m) and then averaged down to 1km. Computing slope at 1km directly would flatten exactly the terrain the model is about. Because the grid is already in metres, no degree-to-metre scale factor enters.
The elevation used for the hydrology is separately pit-filled at 1km: the trusted 300m DEM is already pit-filled, but averaging it down to 1km can create new local minima. D8 flow direction and flow accumulation run on the pit-filled version, and the accumulated pixel count is scaled to an upslope contributing area in m².

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
section: Slope stability with and without forest roots
text:
Slope stability with and without forest roots
The stability model is the infinite-slope form used across the SHALSTAB / SINMAP / TRIGRS family. For every pixel,
\[
SI \;=\; \frac{\tan\phi}{\tan\beta}
\;+\; \frac{c_{\text{soil}} + c_{\text{root}}}{\gamma\,h\,\sin\beta\,\cos\beta}
\;-\; \min\!\left(\frac{q}{T\,\sin\beta},\,1\right)
\]
where \(\phi\) is the internal friction angle, \(\beta\) the slope, \(c_{\text{soil}}\) the soil’s own cohesion, \(c_{\text{root}}\) the root reinforcement, \(\gamma\) the soil unit weight, \(h\) the soil depth, \(q\) the specific discharge and \(T\) the transmissivity. The first term is friction against geometry, the second is cohesion holding the slope together, and the third is the destabilising effect of water. Higher \(SI\) is more stable.
The four soil terms are derived from the mapped soil properties:

Friction angle \(\phi = 25 + (\text{sand}\% - \text{clay}\%)/20\), clipped to 15-40 degrees: sandier soils resist shear at a steeper angle than clay-rich ones.
Soil cohesion \(c_{\text{soil}} = 2 + 0.03\,\text{clay}\% + 0.1\,\text{organic carbon}\%\) kPa, clipped to 0-50 kPa.
Unit weight \(\gamma = \rho\,g\), converting SoilGrids bulk density in Mg/m³ to kN/m³.
Transmissivity \(T = K_{\text{sat}} \times h\), with HiHydroSoil’s integer conductivity unscaled and converted to m/day first.

The specific discharge is static rather than event-based: the WorldClim annual rainfall total is spread evenly over the year, applied to the pixel’s upslope contributing area, and divided by the cell width it enters through. The hydrological term is physically a saturation ratio, so it is capped at 1; uncapped, the heavily right-skewed upslope area drives most pixels onto the stability floor.
Root cohesion is the only thing that differs between the two runs. It is \(c_{\text{root}} = \text{forest share} \times c_{\text{root,max}}\) with \(c_{\text{root,max}} = 5\) kPa in the observed run and \(0\) in the full_impacts counterfactual.
Three exclusions and clips are part of the method rather than defensive coding, and each changes results:

Pixels flatter than 2 degrees are excluded entirely. Infinite-slope theory does not apply there, and without the exclusion both the friction and hydrological terms blow up near \(\beta = 0\) and swamp the forest-cover signal – the median observed-versus-counterfactual difference was exactly zero before it was added.
Slope is clipped to 0.5-89.5 degrees and the friction angle to 15-40 degrees before the trigonometry, since \(\tan\beta\) goes to zero at flat and diverges near vertical.
\(SI\) itself is clipped to \([-10, 10]\).

The observed index is computed for every modelling year and the prediction year; the counterfactual only for the prediction year, since a counterfactual has no meaning during calibration.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Calibrating stability to landslide probability
Recorded landslides are rare relative to land pixels, so the hazard model is fitted on a stratified case-control sample rather than on the whole grid.
Cases are UGLC events. The events are filtered to those with a usable location accuracy – the recorded accuracy must be present, positive, not one of the fill codes UGLC uses, and no coarser than 1000m – and then reprojected to EASE-Grid metres. Several events can fall in one 1km pixel, so within a year they are collapsed to one row per pixel carrying the highest fatality count of the group: the model is fitted on pixel-years.
Controls are pixel-years drawn uniformly at random over the grid and kept only where the GAEZ raster says there is land, at 25 controls per case, with a fixed seed so the draw is reproducible. Each row, case or control, is then sampled for its stability index, annual maximum daily rainfall, population, slope, road density and GAEZ zone. Rows missing stability, rainfall or zone are dropped – most of them are the near-flat pixels the stability model excluded.
An ordinary logit of case status on stability index and extreme rainfall is fitted on the modelling years. Its slope coefficients are consistent estimates of the population slopes, but its intercept carries the oversampling of cases, so it is corrected (Prentice and Pyke 1979):
\[
\alpha_{\text{corrected}} \;=\; \alpha_{\text{raw}} \;-\; \log\!\frac{\tau/(1-\tau)}{\pi/(1-\pi)}
\]
\(\tau\) is the case fraction in the sample. \(\pi\) is the prevalence in the population, and it is not assumed: it is counted from the UGLC annual panels themselves, as event pixel-years over SI-eligible land pixel-years across the same years used for training. Restricting the denominator to the pixels the stability model actually scores keeps the prevalence on the same population the model predicts over. The per-year counts behind it are exported as an audit table.
To build those panels, each UGLC event is stamped onto the grid as a disc of its own location accuracy rather than as a single pixel: the binary panel marks every pixel the disc covers, and the mortality panel spreads the event’s fatalities over the disc with a linear distance decay \(1 - d/r\), summed across events.
The fit is scored by AUC on the training years and on the held-out prediction year.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Fatalities given a landslide
Severity is a two-part hurdle model, fitted only on realized landslides (the cases) in the modelling years, on the same four covariates in both parts: log(1+population), extreme rainfall, slope and road density.

Part A, a logit, gives \(\Pr(\text{fatalities} > 0 \mid \text{landslide})\). If the maximum likelihood fit fails on separation, it falls back to an L2-regularized fit; the coefficients are then shrunk toward zero and the standard errors are not comparable to an unpenalized fit, so that fallback is a point estimate rather than inference.
Part B, an OLS on the fatal subsample, gives \(E[\log(\text{fatalities}) \mid \text{fatal}]\).

Back-transforming part B needs care: \(\exp\) of a predicted log understates the expectation by Jensen’s inequality. The correction is Duan’s (1983) smearing factor, the mean of \(\exp\) of the part-B residuals, which estimates the bias from the residuals themselves rather than assuming log-normal errors. Expected fatalities given a landslide are therefore
\[
E[\text{deaths} \mid \text{landslide}] \;=\;
\Pr(\text{fatal}) \times \exp\!\big(X\beta_B\big) \times \text{smearing}.
\]
A separate diagnostic refits both parts with the stability index in place of slope, to check whether stability subsumes slope’s information in severity. It is written to its own output and never overwrites the production coefficients.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Prediction and avoided mortality
Prediction runs tile by tile over the land-containing tiles of the grid (2000 pixels per side by default), so the global rasters are assembled from independent pieces.
For each scenario, expected deaths per pixel-year are
\[
\text{deaths} \;=\; \Pr(\text{landslide} \mid SI, \text{rain}) \times E[\text{deaths} \mid \text{landslide}].
\]
Rainfall is the prediction year’s, and the severity covariates do not vary by scenario, so the severity expectation is computed once per tile and reused. The scenarios differ only through the stability index that enters the hazard probability – which is to say, only through root cohesion.
Avoided mortality is then the counterfactual minus the observed:
\[
\text{avoided deaths} \;=\; \text{deaths}_{\text{full\_impacts}} \;-\; \text{deaths}_{\text{observed}}.
\]
Physically this cannot be negative – removing root cohesion cannot make a slope safer – so pixels where it comes out negative are counted and warned about rather than silently floored.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Valuation
Avoided deaths are priced at the value of a statistical life, per country, in 2019 constant USD to match the rest of GEP.
Countries with a published OECD country estimate take it directly. The published figures are 2022 USD and are reported with a power-of-ten multiplier, so they are scaled up and then deflated to 2019 using the PMPRB CPI-based cumulative price-adjustment factor of 1.050 from 2019 to 2022.
Countries without a direct estimate take their income group’s figure from Table 6.1 of OECD (2025), Mortality Risk Valuation in Policy Assessment: 7.1 USD million for high-income OECD, 7.9 for high-income non-OECD, and 1.1 for the upper-middle, lower-middle and low-income groups. A row whose income group is unclassified takes the global figure of 2.7 USD million. These are 2022 USD millions and are deflated the same way.
The per-country values are joined onto the EE r264 correspondence and rasterized onto the 1km grid, so every pixel carries its country’s VSL. The service’s value raster is the avoided-death raster times the VSL raster, and country totals are the zonal sums of both rasters over the correspondence polygons.
Note that the r264 correspondence splits large countries into sub-regions. Each sub-region carries its country’s ISO3 and therefore its national VSL, which is what the rasterization needs; a one-row-per-country table has to sum the sub-regions back together, which is what the results report does.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
section: What the module does not do
text:
What the module does not do

The stability model is static: one specific discharge from a climatological rainfall normal, not an event-based or seasonal hydrology.
Rainfall enters the hazard model as the annual maximum daily total, so hazard is a per-pixel-year probability, not a per-storm one.
Transmissivity units are flagged as unverified in the code and have not been checked against the HiHydroSoil documentation here.
The module has been run end to end once on the cluster, but its numbers have not been replicated against a machine-readable v0.2.0 output from the author, so they remain provisional.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
References
The citations below are the ones the code itself names. They are the model family and the specific corrections applied, not a general literature review.

Duan, N. (1983). Smearing estimate: a nonparametric retransformation method.
Horn, B. K. P. (1981). Hill shading and the reflectance map. (The slope algorithm gdal.DEMProcessing uses.)
OECD (2025). Mortality Risk Valuation in Policy Assessment, Table 6.1.
Prentice, R. L., and Pyke, R. (1979). Logistic disease incidence models and case-control studies.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Coastal Protection
text: This section outlines how we value coastal protection as an ecosystem service within the GEP framework. Coastal habitats reduce the energy of waves and storm surge before it reaches the shore, so property and infrastructure behind them suffer less damage than they would on a bare coast. The service is therefore valued as avoided storm and flood damage, and it is reported for two habitats: mangroves and coral reefs. Both are attributed to the country whose coast they protect, and the two components are added to give one national coastal protection value.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Coastal Protection
text:
Estimating Quantity
Neither component is modelled from habitat extent inside this module. Both arrive as published per-country tables in which the physical protection modelling has already been done upstream, so the quantity stage here is the read and the aggregation onto the country list rather than a biophysical calculation.
Mangroves. The mangrove component is the World Bank Changing Wealth of Nations mangrove table, staged as data_mangroves_2019.xlsx. It carries, per country, the mangrove area in hectares, a protection value per hectare, and the annual protection value that is their product, all for 2019 and all in current US dollars. The model reads the annual value column. Because the table is keyed on the r264 country label, a country that the correspondence splits into sub-regions arrives as several rows, and those rows are summed so that each country ends up with exactly one value.
Coral reefs. The coral component is the annual expected flood protection benefit table staged as coral_reefs_annual_expected_benefit_nfamara.xlsx, which gives one annual benefit per country in 2011 US dollars. This table is keyed on country name rather than country code, so it is joined to the correspondence on the name and then reduced to one row per country before the currency conversion below.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Coastal Protection
text:
Estimating Price
No price is applied in this module. Both source tables are already monetary, which means the quantity and price stages are fused upstream and the attribution factor is one:
\[
\text{GEP}_{\text{coastal protection}} = Q \cdot P \cdot \lambda = \text{avoided damage} \times 1 \times 1
\]
The only monetary adjustment made here is a currency year alignment. The mangrove table is already in the base year’s dollars and needs none. The coral table is in 2011 dollars, so each country’s value is multiplied by the cumulative World Bank GDP deflator for that country over 2012 through 2019 (the annual series NY.GDP.DEFL.KD.ZG, where each year contributes a factor of one plus its rate divided by one hundred, and the eight years are multiplied together).

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Coastal Protection
text:
Valuation
The two components are joined on country and year, a country present in only one table contributes that component alone, and the national value is their sum:
\[
\text{GEP}_{\text{coastal protection},c} = V^{\text{mangrove}}_{c,2019} + V^{\text{coral}}_{c,2011} \cdot D_{c,2012 \rightarrow 2019}
\]
where \(V^{\text{mangrove}}_{c,2019}\) is the country’s annual mangrove protection value in 2019 dollars, \(V^{\text{coral}}_{c,2011}\) is its annual coral reef protection benefit in 2011 dollars, and \(D_{c,2012 \rightarrow 2019}\) is its cumulative GDP deflator over that span. The result is written as one row per country for the base year 2019, with the two components kept as separate columns beside the total so that either can be inspected on its own.
On the currently staged input data this gives a global total of \(36.72\) billion in 2019 US dollars, of which \(30.40\) billion is the mangrove component and \(6.32\) billion is the coral reef component.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Coastal Protection
text:
Known limitations
Three properties of the calculation are worth stating because they affect coverage rather than arithmetic, and none of them is silent once you know to look for it.
The coral table is joined on country name, not on a code. A name that the correspondence spells differently would drop the country without failing, so the join is a place to check first when a coastal country is missing.
A country the World Bank deflator series does not cover has no multiplier, so its coral value cannot be carried to the base year and the country comes out unvalued rather than valued at zero. On the currently staged data this affects nine countries holding about $75 million of 2011 coral value: the Cook Islands, Guadeloupe, Martinique, Mayotte, Niue, Pitcairn, Réunion, Taiwan and Wallis and Futuna. None of the nine carries a mangrove value either, so their rows now read as missing and the reported global total is unchanged.
Because the module consumes pre-valued national tables, it cannot separate the physical extent of a habitat from the value assigned to it. A change in either the mapped habitat area or the damage function behind these tables enters here only as a changed national total.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
Turn the pipeline’s own 300 m SEALS land-use maps into a per-region, per-year crop-productivity shock for the eight crop sectors (PDR, WHT, GRO, V_F, OSD, C_B, PFB, OCR), so the economic model responds to the soil protection each scenario’s land cover actually provides rather than to a frozen table.
Land cover enters soil loss only through the cover-management factor, so scenario differences in this module are land-driven by construction.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
Turn the pipeline’s own 300 m SEALS land-use maps into a per-region, per-year crop-productivity shock for the eight crop sectors (PDR, WHT, GRO, V_F, OSD, C_B, PFB, OCR), so the economic model responds to the soil protection each scenario’s land cover actually provides rather than to a frozen table.
Land cover enters soil loss only through the cover-management factor, so scenario differences in this module are land-driven by construction.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
Method
The biophysics is InVEST’s Sediment Delivery Ratio model, run per scenario and anchor year. It yields two rasters that everything downstream is built from: USLE, the soil loss under actual land cover, and RKLS, the loss the same pixel would suffer bare. Their difference is the erosion the land cover prevents.
Turning that into an economic shock needs a coefficient linking erosion to yield. No method avoids this, so it is the key calibration for erosion regardless of which variant is used.
We report two formulations side by side, because they answer different questions and neither is strictly better.

A, “damage” (the conservative reading)
Only severe erosion is assumed to harm yield. A pixel is severe where USLE exceeds a per-country soil-loss tolerance: 2 t/ha/yr for small or low-lying countries, 11 otherwise. Cropland is SEALS7 class 2. For each zone,
\[\text{level}_A = -100 \, \alpha \, p_{crop}, \qquad p_{crop} = \frac{\text{severe cropland area}}{\text{total cropland area}}\]
with a single flat \(\alpha\). This is thresholded, binary, on-farm only, and weighted by cropland area. Because land cover carries no crop detail, method A is necessarily uniform across sectors , it cannot tell wheat land from vegetable land.


B, “service” (the comprehensive reading)
All erosion prevention counts, everywhere on cropland, and off-site protection is included. The prevention share combines the on-farm fraction \(1 - \text{USLE}/\text{RKLS}\) with an upstream term obtained by D8 flow-accumulating prevented and potential mass, so vegetation upslope is credited for the sediment it stops reaching land below.
Two properties matter. The zone average is magnitude-weighted: it aggregates tonnes, not percentages, as prevented over potential production-weighted mass. Without this, a pixel preventing 90 % of almost no erosion would count as much as one preventing 40 % of a great deal. And the coefficient is per crop, so a crop’s own erosion sensitivity is applied to its own prevention share before production-weighting across crops.
\[\text{level}_B = 100 \sum_c w_c \, \alpha_c \, \frac{\text{prevented}_c}{\text{potential}_c} \Big/ \sum_c w_c\]
Because crops are mapped to GTAP sectors, B reports a different shock per sector: a zone eroding mainly under cereals sends that signal to GRO rather than spreading it across all eight.


Sign conventions
A measures damage borne and is negative; B measures protection delivered and is positive. This does not affect the shock, because the two differ by a constant that cancels when the baseline is subtracted.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
From level to shock
Each level is already a percentage of crop productivity, so the shock is the absolute difference against the contemporaneous baseline (the nature-off counterfactual in the same year) not a relative change. That difference is zero at the base year and interpolated linearly between the 5-year anchors, then applied as a factor-productivity term (afeall).
A third level is also emitted for comparison and never fed to the economic model: the same prevention share kept behind A’s severe-pixel gate and weighted by production alone. It differs from B only in how exposure is measured, which makes it a useful check on how much the threshold and the weighting matter.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
Crop coefficients
The per-crop coefficients come from a table of erosion-to-yield sensitivities keyed by FAO item names, joined to IFPRI SPAM crop groups. The join is one-to-many in places, since SPAM’s 46 groups are coarser than FAO’s item list, so a few resolutions are representative substitutions rather than exact matches (all citrus through oranges, all temperate fruit through apples, pigeon pea through dry peas). Four SPAM aggregates have no FAO counterpart and inherit their sector’s mean; for other cereals that gives 0.30, matching every named cereal in the table.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
Static fallback
When a service is not listed in dynamic_es, the same seam grafts a static task that reads the frozen per-scenario dependency table instead. That table carries a single 2050 endpoint computed on older land cover, so intermediate years are a synthetic ramp rather than real per-year values, which is why the dynamic path exists.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
Compute
The SDR model is multi-hour and memory-heavy per global map, so resolution follows the run modality: a 6.45 km analysis grid locally, native SEALS resolution on a cluster. run_erosion.py runs the calculation standalone, which is the practical way to iterate on it without invoking the economic model.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text: Fire protection asks how much wildfire damage is avoided because fires do not persist as strongly where nature dominates. The calculation is ported function by function from the GEP wildfire repository’s R pipeline, gep_wildfire_2019.R. The base year is 2019 and the price convention recorded in es_config.csv is avoided damage.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text:
Quantity
Burned acres avoided or added in 2019.
The persistence side comes from per-country AR(1) regressions, burned area on its own one-year lag, of burned area on its own one-year lag, run upstream with the results committed as a CSV. build_regression_type_ids filters the regressions the GEP does not read and assigns each remaining one a type id. compute_beta_differences then reads three quantities off the wide table:

the baseline persistence effect, total burned area on its own lag over the full sample,
the nature-versus-human cause difference, nature-caused fires’ persistence minus human-caused fires’,
the nature-versus-human area difference, persistence in nature-dominated minus human-dominated districts.

The two differences use difference_stats, which takes the difference of two independent estimates, combines their standard errors in quadrature, and reports the two-sided normal approximation p-value. A difference is computed only where all four inputs are present.
compute_avoided_acres converts each beta to marginal additional acres by multiplying by HA_TO_ACRES, then to 2019 additional acres by multiplying by the country’s 2018 burned hectares.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text:
Price
EM-DAT wildfire damages per burned acre, by country. read_emdat_wildfire_damages sums the total adjusted damage column, which the source workbook stores in thousands of USD with comma separators, over wildfire events per ISO3. compute_damage_per_acre divides that by the country’s burned acres across all panel years and fills any country whose rate is zero or missing with the global average over countries with positive rates.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text:
Valuation
compute_gep multiplies the two together and flips the sign, because additional acres carry the persistence sign and the value of avoiding them is the negative product:
\[
\text{GEP}_{\text{variant}} = -\,\text{additional acres 2019}_{\text{variant}} \times \text{damages per acre}
\]
Countries absent from the damage-rate merge take the global average, as in the source.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the fire_protection service:

fire_regression_results_path, the committed per-country AR(1) regression results.
fire_emdat_path, the EM-DAT custom request workbook.
fire_panel_path, the burned-area panel at GADM’s second administrative level, one row per district per year, with a _source_note row recording that it comes from the drive’s Wildfires folder.

reference/GEP_wildfire_2019_results.csv ships inside the module as the frozen replication anchor.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text:
Outputs
beta_differences.csv, avoided_acres.csv and damage_per_acre.csv, each from its own task, then two files from gep_calculation. fire_protection_2019_results.csv keeps the source repo’s column shape so it can be diffed against the committed output. gep_by_country_base_year.csv holds the r250 identifiers and attributes, year, the three variant columns GEP_wildfire_2019_baseline, GEP_wildfire_2019_nn_hh and GEP_wildfire_2019_ttn_tth, and fire_protection_gep. All three variant totals are logged.
GID_0 is already an iso3 country label, so the r250 attributes join by label and nothing is summed in the collapse.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text:
Method constants

HA_TO_ACRES = 2.47105.
FIRE_BASELINE_ID = 3, FIRE_NN_ID = 2 and FIRE_HH_ID = 1, FIRE_TTN_ID = 6 and FIRE_TTH_ID = 7, which select the betas for the three variants.
FIRE_DROP_Y_VARS, the fifteen days, counts and average variants the source drops before ids are assigned.
FIRE_GEP_PROVISIONAL_VARIANT = 'nn_hh' in the tasks module, the variant fire_protection_gep currently carries.
significance_level thresholds, 3 stars below p 0.01, 2 below 0.05, 1 below 0.10, otherwise 0.

FIRE_REG_TYPES records the five regression-type ids the GEP reads together with the (Y_var, Key_X_var, sample) triple each id must carry.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text:
Faithful-port notes
Two behaviours are reproduced rather than corrected, so the port stays comparable against the anchor.
The source pivots the regression table with a mean aggregator over every value column, including the character significance stars. R’s mean() on character returns NA, so every wide significance column, and therefore every *_signif_level in the output, is 0 by construction. The p-value columns beside them are real.
Beta selection is by regression-type id, which in the source is data.table’s .GRP, the first-appearance order of the triple in the input CSV. A reordered input would silently reassign the betas, so build_regression_type_ids asserts the expected triples and raises before any beta is read.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text:
Taken as given
The AR(1) regressions themselves, which are run upstream and consumed here as a committed results table. The committed per-country output reproduces to the float, which the test suite pins.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text:
What is open
Which of the three variants is the account’s fire protection value. Baseline and nature-versus-human cause both total negative globally, so the choice sets both the number and its interpretation. fire_protection_gep defaults to the nature-versus-human cause difference provisionally.
The ADM2 burned-area panel is not staged, and its own README says it lives on the drive. Until it arrives, the 2018 burned areas and the damage rates are read from the frozen reference output, with a loud log line each time, so the beta science and everything downstream still run and verify on any machine.

title: Marine-fisheries ecosystem-service shock
text: Provide a per-region, per-year productivity shock for the fisheries sector (FSH), so the economic model responds to how climate alters marine fish productivity along each scenario’s pathway.

title: Marine-fisheries ecosystem-service shock
text: Provide a per-region, per-year productivity shock for the fisheries sector (FSH), so the economic model responds to how climate alters marine fish productivity along each scenario’s pathway.

title: Marine-fisheries ecosystem-service shock
text:
Why this service is different
The other three services are computed from the pipeline’s own 300 m SEALS land-use maps. Fisheries is marine: its productivity is not a function of terrestrial land cover, so nothing in the SEALS output can inform it. It therefore has no dynamic-from-maps variant, and dynamic_es does not apply to it , the seam grafts one task either way.
This is a property of the service, not a gap in the implementation. A shock keyed to sea-surface conditions cannot be derived from a land-cover map.

title: Marine-fisheries ecosystem-service shock
text:
Method
Fish productivity change is taken from pre-computed marine projections, stored as FI26, FI45 and FI85 headers in cwon_shocks.har, one per representative concentration pathway. Each scenario is matched to the header for the pathway closest to its temperature trajectory, the same RCP keying used for the climate crop-yield shock, so the marine and terrestrial climate signals stay consistent.
Values are read per year over the horizon rather than frozen at an endpoint. For the current data this is equivalent to a constant, because the underlying series steps once and then plateaus across 2023–2050; time-varying projections would flow through unchanged.

title: Marine-fisheries ecosystem-service shock
text:
Capping
The shock is capped at ±2 %. This is deliberately tight and exists for a specific reason: one region’s FI26 value is an order of magnitude larger than any other region’s, and inconsistent with that same region’s own values under the other two pathways. Every legitimate value falls well inside the cap, so in practice the cap clips exactly one implausible entry and touches nothing else. It is a guard against a known data artefact, not a general-purpose smoother, and the underlying value should be corrected at source.

title: Marine-fisheries ecosystem-service shock
text:
From level to shock
The per-year values are applied to FSH for each region, zero at the base year and interpolated across the horizon. Fisheries enters the economic model as an output-augmenting term, unlike the terrestrial services which enter as factor-productivity terms.

title: Marine-fisheries ecosystem-service shock
text:
Compute
Trivial, the task reads binary headers and writes a CSV, taking seconds. run_fisheries.py runs it standalone, needing only cwon_shocks.har for the configured aggregation.

title: GEP service library: status
text:
This drives the service status. Change the prose here, then run python3 docs/publish_service_status.py to refresh the group’s shared sheet from it.
Refactoring onto the library template means every service is built the same way, in two files.
One file holds the maths and never opens or saves anything. The second file does the opening and saving. It reads the input data, calls the maths, and writes the results.
Every service joins its results to the same country list and builds its results page the same way.
The fields mean: category is what the code does to produce the number, on a scale from reading a published value to running a model here. method is how the number is computed. ours is whether we can compute the number ourselves, or only read someone else’s. code is the engineering work we did. number is what the figure is and what it was checked against. need is what we are waiting on from someone else. signed off is whether the service meets the nine conditions below.
What signed off means.
The standard the account is built to: somebody who wants to reproduce a GEP number should be able to read this repository and follow every step, without opening anyone else’s. They will need the data — base_data holds inputs from many authors and always will — but not another codebase, and not a person to explain the missing part.
That is what signed off: green asserts. Nine conditions, each of which has already failed somewhere and been caught:
Green means all nine. amber means the number is usable and at least one condition is open, with the entry saying which. red means the number should not be quoted yet.
⚠ A service can be green while its check is fidelity-only, provided condition 5 is met and the entry says so. Green is a statement about our engineering being complete and legible, not a claim that the science is right.
The five categories, in ascending order of what the code does.
1. Reads a published value — 1 account. The per-country figure already exists in a file. We open it and reshape it to the house table, and no valuation happens. Urban cooling is the one: the city-month valuations are ours, but the reported figure is parsed from a dollar column in a committed file.
2. Rescales a published rate — 2 accounts. Someone published a rate rather than a value, and one or two operations turn it into dollars. Mining production is a rent share times GDP times 0.49; extractive energy is the sum of three published per-fuel rent columns. Real arithmetic, but the economics is entirely theirs.
3. Table arithmetic — 12 accounts. A quantity, a price and an attribution multiplied over tables, with no grids involved. This is the bulk of the library: crop production, livestock, both fisheries rows, energy production, hydropower, water use, air filtration, sandstorm prevention, wildfires, water quality and coastal protection.
4. Raster arithmetic — 7 accounts. The value cannot be reached without processing grids, cell by cell, multiplied and summed into countries. Pollination multiplies 158 production grids by price and by each crop’s pollinator dependence per cell; terrestrial carbon builds density rasters. Also coastal carbon, ntfp, timber, floods and stormwater.
5. Process model run here — 3 accounts. A model with dynamics of its own runs inside the pipeline. Erosion runs InVEST SDR with sediment routing, landslides computes slope stability twice for every pixel, and recreation runs a gravity model allocating visits into scored sites.
category and ours answer different questions. A service can run a model here and still not be ours, because the coefficients or the physical quantity come from elsewhere. Wildfires is the clearest case: the valuation runs here, and the regression coefficients underneath it do not.
The ladder measures work, not confidence. Read as a quality ranking it gets things backwards. The account without a usable number sits at the top of it: stormwater reports retained volume and no dollar total because its price is a placeholder of 1. Crop production, down at table arithmetic, reproduces its reference table exactly.
One label per service hides a split. Several services compute part of the value and read the rest, and the category can only name the heaviest thing the code does. Water quality computes its dollar figure and reads the international-dollar one it reports; coastal protection computes the mangrove half and reads the coral half; ntfp computes the accessible area and reads the value per hectare. ours is where that lives.

title: GEP service library: status
text:
Terrestrial Carbon

subgroup: terrestrial
module: terrestrial_carbon
category: raster arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: yes
method: Carbon density by climate zone and land-cover class, times hectares per cell, summed to countries, times the rental social cost of carbon. Rental is not the full social cost: the full cost is what a tonne is worth as an asset, and the rental is one year’s service from holding it. The account is an annual flow, so it takes the yearly service. The rental is P(1 - e^-r), which at 2 percent turns an asset worth $665.87 a tonne of carbon into $13.19 a year. The quantity is a carbon density raster built here from a zone-by-class density table and the land-cover map.
total: $5.365T
code: Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Corrected division by the wrong baseline for the shock, and corrected a double-count that had entered split countries once per sub-region.
grid: WGS84 geographic on the shared 10 arc-second pyramid. Cell area is the per-latitude ha_per_cell raster, multiplied into the density in terrestrial_carbon_tasks.py:146. Correct: a geographic grid needs a per-cell area and this carries one.
reference: The manuscript total. NOT independent of us in the part that matters, since we reproduce a figure computed from the same density table and land-cover map. The double-count we fixed was ours to find, which is what an agreement of this kind cannot surface.
replicated: Yes, the manuscript total. ⚠ Same lineage, so it tests our port rather than the science.
decided: -
number: Values the carbon stored in land ecosystems, priced at the rental social cost of carbon. Reproduces the manuscript total of $5.365T, after fixing a double-count that entered split countries once per sub-region (China six times, 23.5 percent overstatement). Priced at the rental social cost of carbon at 2 percent. The 3 percent sensitivity is a run of its own and gives $3.4627T. There is no 1 percent column.
need: Two decisions on the discount rate. First, whether carbon prices are taken to grow. The r in the rental formula is the net rate, the discount rate minus the growth rate of carbon prices, so our 2 percent column assumes prices do not grow. The table already carries the alternative: a column at 3 percent discounting minus 2.2 percent growth, so 0.8 percent net, which gives $2.29 a tonne against our $13.19. Second, the 1 percent price. It cannot be derived from carbon_prices.xlsx, which holds only $181.60 per tonne of CO2 at 2 percent and $78.53 at 3 percent. Not clear where they came from.
signed off: amber: examined, and at least one of the eight conditions is not yet verified ## Coastal Carbon
subgroup: coastal
module: coastal_carbon
category: raster arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: yes
method: Mapped mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass area, times carbon density per habitat and pool, priced like terrestrial carbon. The quantity is habitat area measured here from the mapped mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass extents.
total: $22.84bn seaward only. $102.18bn both sides.
code: Merged the author’s rework, then refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Checked the refactored code against the original on identical inputs.
grid: WGS84 geographic on the shared pyramid, cell area from ha_per_cell. ⚠ The grid was never the problem here. Its extent was: a 0/1 mask credited a habitat with every cell it touched, putting mangrove at 29.08 Mha against 14.69 Mha of polygon and salt marsh near three times its area. Mangrove and salt marsh now weight each cell by the share the habitat covers. ⚠ Seagrass does NOT, because its density is a polygon attribute, so it still sums polygon areas that overlap.
reference: The author’s reported numbers. ⚠ That agreement held while the extent was roughly doubled, so it never tested the extent. The coverage fix moves mangrove -48.8 percent and salt marsh -66.1 percent, and the EEZ-only total from $22.84bn to $17.72bn. Yanxu has not yet been told.
