title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Vegetated landscapes intercept rainfall, slow its passage into rivers and store part of it in the soil. Where they do so upstream of towns and farmland, floods downstream are shallower than they would otherwise be, and the damage those floods cause is smaller. That reduction in damage is what this account values.
The scope is river flooding only. Coastal flooding, storm surge and pluvial flooding lie outside it, following the hazard product the account uses. Coverage is 250 countries at 537 m, reported in USD 2019.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Vegetated landscapes intercept rainfall, slow its passage into rivers and store part of it in the soil. Where they do so upstream of towns and farmland, floods downstream are shallower than they would otherwise be, and the damage those floods cause is smaller. That reduction in damage is what this account values.
The scope is river flooding only. Coastal flooding, storm surge and pluvial flooding lie outside it, following the hazard product the account uses. Coverage is 250 countries at 537 m, reported in USD 2019.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Method
Valuing this service requires answering a question that cannot be observed: how much flood damage would occur if landscapes stopped absorbing rain. The account simulates a counterfactual world in which ecosystems no longer retain water, routes the same storms through it, and takes the difference.
Everything turns on one number per location, the depth amplification: the ratio of flood depth in the degraded world to flood depth in the current one. Hydrology has no standard name for it, because it has not previously been needed – it exists here only because there is a paired counterfactual world to run.

Step 1, how absorbent each piece of land is
A curve number between 30 and 100 is assigned to every cell by crossing land cover with soil hydrologic group, from USDA field measurements:
\[S = 25400 / \text{CN} - 254\]
\(S\) is the potential maximum retention in millimetres. Forest on loam holds 208 mm; the same soil stripped bare holds 41 mm. This is the only point in the account where vegetation enters the physics.


Step 2, how much extra water runs off
\[I_a = 0.2S, \qquad Q = (P - I_a)^2 / (P - I_a + S) \text{ for } P > I_a\]
The relation saturates. As \(P\) grows large relative to \(S\), runoff approaches total rainfall regardless of land cover, so the service is concentrated in frequent events and the largest proportional effects appear where storms are small relative to what the soil can hold.


Step 3, following the water downhill
\[\text{ratio}(i) = \text{accum}(Q_\text{degraded})(i) / \text{accum}(Q_\text{current})(i)\]
Routing uses MERIT Hydro. On the Upper Mississippi, seven per cent more runoff at the point of rainfall becomes twenty-two per cent more discharge in the river: routing roughly triples the local effect, and that is what makes flood regulation a landscape service rather than a local one.


Step 4, turning more water into deeper water
\[A(i) = [\text{ratio}(i)]^{f}, \qquad f \approx 0.4\]
At-a-station hydraulic geometry gives the split between width, depth and velocity. So 21.5% more discharge produces 8% more depth. The exponent is the least constrained element of the chain and is swept over 0.3 to 0.5.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Two counterfactuals
Bare soil removes land cover entirely, setting curve numbers to the fallow values of the reference tables. This is the world a gross product asks about, and it is the reference the erosion account uses, so the two services are measured against one hypothetical landscape and can be summed.
In-situ degradation raises curve numbers less: soils compacted and canopy thinned, the land still present. Closer to what realistic degradation would produce, and reported alongside rather than as a sensitivity.
Bare soil exceeds in-situ by about 2.5, and that ratio is stable to within four per cent across both hazard products and both treatments of permanent water.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Lambda
Lambda is 1 for this service. The counterfactual already isolates the ecosystem contribution: it is a difference between two worlds identical in every respect except the ecosystem, so whatever remains in the difference is the ecosystem’s doing by construction.
The prevention share reported throughout is a different quantity and not an attribution coefficient:
\[\text{prevention share} = (\text{EAD}_\text{degraded} - \text{EAD}_\text{current}) / \text{EAD}_\text{degraded}\]
An attribution share near 1 and a prevention share near 0.01 are not two estimates of one thing.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Sign conventions
GEP is positive: it is damage that does not occur. Degradation raises expected annual damage, so the difference is non-negative by construction and a negative value indicates a routing or alignment fault rather than a result.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Compute
The amplification field is built from rainfall and flow direction rather than from the hazard maps, so it survives a change of hazard product. Building it is two weeks of single-threaded flow accumulation over 75 billion cells; everything downstream of it is hours. RUN.md documents both paths.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
section: Before trusting any rerun of the pipeline
text:
Before trusting any rerun of the pipeline
The account as it stands does not rerun the pipeline: gep_calculation reads the author’s own per-country export, so the number here is his verified one. This section matters only if that changes.

The failure that made this account wrong twice
The author’s RUN.md is explicit, and it is the most important thing in it:

Check flow-direction coverage. This is not optional, and it is the reason this account was wrong twice.

Seven MERIT flow-direction packages were missing at various points, and every absence was silent. Accumulation over a missing network writes nodata, the amplification clips to a minimum of 1.0, and the valuation reads 1.0 as no change here rather than no data here. Japan, Korea, Portugal and Kazakhstan returned zero service against 49 bn USD of exposure; Nigeria, Chad, Cameroon, Niger and the Central African Republic another 4 bn. Nothing in any log recorded a problem. Both were found because a country looked implausible. Recovering them raised GEP by 18.5 per cent and then a further 16.
python prep_merit_dir.py --check-tiles
⚠ The check has a limit the author states plainly. Its reference list was generated from a tile set believed complete, so it detects regressions — a lost file, a partial copy, an interrupted extraction — but not a package that was never downloaded, which was the original failure.
A missing amplification raster behaves the same way: the pipeline warns, falls back to current depths and returns a GEP of zero, so the job completes and the number is wrong. RUN.md carries a three-line check that the mosaic resolves, and msi/final_run.sbatch verifies the totals itself and prints ALL MATCH or the quantity that differs.


The account should compute this itself
⚠ Reading the author’s per-country export is an interim, not the destination.
Not because every service computes its own — about a third do not, and for some that is right: the account does not recompute the World Bank’s CWON resource rents for extractive materials or energy, because the published rent is the source. The distinction is whether we hold a model we could run.
Flood’s peers are stormwater and air filtration, both recorded as “not yet”: a model that exists, that we have, and that has not been run here. Erosion is the case to follow — it has no scenario shock either, and it still runs the sediment model here and reports $13.96bn against the author’s $14.59bn.
The distinction worth keeping: producing our own number is what the library is for, and it is what makes the figure reproducible, auditable and rerunnable here. Comparing it to the author’s is a fidelity check and not a correctness one. The second does not argue against the first.
Until then, gep_calculation reads flood_gep_for_merge_v2_2024hazard.csv and the account carries his $11.40bn. That is honest and it is not finished.


What running it needs
The inputs are on MSI at /projects/standard/jajohns/shared/flood_gep, read-only, so a run needs a writable root with those inputs linked in and the Sections B and C rasters copied across — about 1 GB, without which a run rebuilds them and takes eleven hours rather than three. In this library the root is flood_root_dir in es_parameters.csv rather than the source repo’s GEP_FLOOD_ROOT environment variable, so only the linking and copying carry over.
⚠ Not done as of 2026-08-28. Nothing here has been run; the account reads his export.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text: Non-timber forest products cover what forests yield other than wood. The account values them per hectare of forest people can actually reach. The base year is 2019 and the price convention recorded in es_config.csv is value per accessible hectare.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Quantity
Hectares of accessible forest. Forest is the ESA CCI class range 50 to 90 inclusive. Accessible means inside a 10 km buffer around roads and rivers. The source repository, geo_ntfp, implements that intersection two ways, a vector-buffer calculation and a distance-raster calculation, and commits no output from either. The library therefore runs both variants and presents both, following the pattern fire protection uses for its variants.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Price
The CWoN 2024 non-wood forest product value per hectare per country, in current USD, read at the GEP base year.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Valuation
ntfp_gep_by_country filters the value series to the base year, joins it onto the accessible-area table by country label, and multiplies:
\[
\text{NTFP GEP} = \text{accessible forest (ha)} \times \text{NWFP value (USD/ha)}
\]
The function is in place and unit-tested.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the ntfp service:

ntfp_roads_region1_path, the GRIP4 Region 1 vector geodatabase, with a _source_url row pointing at the public PBL download.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Output
gep_by_country_base_year.csv in the gep_calculation task directory, holding the country label, the accessible forest hectares, the value per hectare and ntfp_gep. It is not yet produced.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Method constants

NTFP_ACCESS_BUFFER_M = 10_000, the accessibility buffer around roads and rivers.
ESA_FOREST_CLASS_MIN = 50 and ESA_FOREST_CLASS_MAX = 90, the inclusive ESA CCI forest class range.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Taken as given
The CWoN NWFP value-per-hectare series.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
What is open
The accessibility raster stage is being ported and is not yet built, so gep_calculation raises NotImplementedError naming exactly what is missing rather than emitting a partial number.
The committed roads file is unusable, because only the sidecar files were committed and the .shp itself never was. The accessibility stage therefore runs on a public global roads dataset, and the original roads file remains a replication ask.
The CWoN value-per-hectare table has no es_parameters.csv row yet, so the price side of the valuation has no recorded path.

title: Pollination ecosystem-service shock
text:
Turn the pipeline’s own 300 m SEALS land-use maps into a per-region, per-year pollination productivity shock for the crop sectors (V_F, OSD), so the economic model responds to the pollinator habitat each scenario actually produces rather than to a frozen table.
The science is William Sidemo-Holm’s crop_benefits package, imported unchanged. This module only drives it per scenario on our maps and aggregates the result to GTAP regions.

title: Pollination ecosystem-service shock
text:
Turn the pipeline’s own 300 m SEALS land-use maps into a per-region, per-year pollination productivity shock for the crop sectors (V_F, OSD), so the economic model responds to the pollinator habitat each scenario actually produces rather than to a frozen table.
The science is William Sidemo-Holm’s crop_benefits package, imported unchanged. This module only drives it per scenario on our maps and aggregates the result to GTAP regions.

title: Pollination ecosystem-service shock
text:
Method
For each scenario, at each SEALS anchor year:

Sufficiency (300 m). For every cropland pixel, count natural-habitat pixels within a ~2 km latitude-adjusted elliptical kernel and normalise against a 30 % habitat threshold, giving a 0–1 sufficiency index (≥30 % habitat nearby → 1; 15 % → 0.5; none → 0). SEALS7 classes: cropland = 2, natural habitat = {3, 4, 5}. The ellipse (rather than a circle) keeps the foraging radius ~2 km on the ground as longitude degrees shorten away from the equator.
Stable cropland. Sufficiency is computed only on pixels that are cropland in both the baseline and the scenario map. This isolates the change in pollinator support on continuously farmed land and excludes land that converted into or out of cropland, matching the original PNAS/InVEST pollination_shock() treatment. Each scenario therefore produces its own paired baseline raster as well as its own scenario raster.
Aggregate to 5 km. Average the 300 m index onto the CropGrids 5 km grid (over stable-ag sub-pixels only), the resolution at which crop production and value are known.
Value. Multiply 5 km sufficiency by the fixed global pollination-value raster (poll_value_global_<base_year>usd.tif, pollination-dependent crop value). The value raster is the same in every scenario, so all scenario variation enters through sufficiency.
Difference. Scenario value minus paired-baseline value, on the 5 km grid.
Regional shock. Area-weighted zonal aggregation to GTAP r50 × AEZ18 zones: (Σ difference × area) / (Σ baseline value × area) × 100, i.e. the percentage change in supported pollination value per zone.
Nature effect. Subtract the corresponding value for the baseline_ignore_dependencies scenario, so the shock isolates the nature signal rather than the shared climate/land trend.
Annual series. The per-anchor-year shocks are interpolated piecewise-linearly (numpy.interp) to annual values, anchored at 0 in the base year (all scenarios share the base-year land, so the shock is zero there by construction). Computing at every SEALS anchor year (rather than only at the horizon) lets the series follow non-linear land trajectories instead of assuming a single straight ramp.

title: Pollination ecosystem-service shock
text:
Output
pollination_interpolated.csv with columns ENDW, ACTS, REG, scenario, year, shock_pct, shock_pct_contemp, shock_pct_fixedbase, written into the shared ES-shock directory (p.es_shock_dir). The downstream build_combined_afeall_cc_es step consumes it unchanged and is agnostic to whether the shock was computed dynamically (as here) or, for other services, read from a precomputed table.

title: Pollination ecosystem-service shock
text:
Inputs







Input
Source




Scenario LULC (300 m, SEALS7)
pipeline’s stitched SEALS maps, one per scenario × anchor year


Baseline LULC (300 m, SEALS7)
pipeline’s SEALS7 base-year map


poll_value_global_<base_year>usd.tif
crop_benefits precomputed baseline value raster


ee_r50_aez18_correspondence.gpkg
GTAP r50 × AEZ18 region boundaries



The FAO / CropGrids / Monfreda stages are not run on the shock side: they build the baseline value raster, which is fixed across scenarios, so the finished raster is used directly here.
They are run on the GEP side, where the account needs the value raster for a base year rather than a scenario. That chain is ours, in pollination_tasks.py, and it is the author’s method rather than a second one:

FAO panel. Filter the FAOSTAT production bulk to Yield and Production over 1993–2024 for the crop items in the FAO classification (run_fao_production).
Yield-change ratios. Median FAO yield in a window at the base year over a window at 2000, per country and crop, with subregion, region and world medians alongside for the countries FAO does not report (fao_yield_change).
Yield rasters. Monfreda’s 2000 yields aligned to the CropGrids grid, gaps filled from the nearest valid cell in the same country, then each country rescaled so its area-weighted mean matches the FAO number for the base year (pollination_yield_rasters).
Production rasters. Yield times CropGrids harvested area, written as tonnes per square kilometre (pollination_production_rasters).
Value raster. Production times the world producer price we build ourselves times each crop’s dependence on animal pollination, with coffee blended per country from what it grows.

Checked against the author’s own 2019 rasters on 2026-08-30: the FAO panel matches his row for row, and global production over 157 crops is 9,008.3 million tonnes on both sides.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation and Tourism
text:
Recreation and tourism are valued at travel cost. The calculation scores every 1 km cell for how good a recreation site it would be, generates visits into the best sites with a gravity model, and prices those visits at what the trip costs in fuel. Residents supply daily recreation and allocated UNWTO overnights supply tourism, through the same engine. The base year is 2019, which is also the UNWTO overnight target year and the fuel-cost price year. The price convention recorded in es_config.csv is travel cost.
The method constants below are the published science, so they live in code. Changing one is a reviewed commit rather than an edit to a project’s input/ copy.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation and Tourism
text:
Site quality
environment_class_array takes the six SEALS7 land-cover class shares, weights them by their recreation scores, adds the protected-area share, and bins the result into an environment class 0 to 3.
accessibility_class_array bins the urban share into a class 0 to 4 and the distance to road into a class 0 to 4, then reads an accessibility class 1 to 5 out of RECREATION_URBAN_ROAD_MATRIX.
site_rank_array crosses the two through RECREATION_SITE_MATRIX into a site rank 1 to 9. extract_high_quality_sites keeps rank 9, and every visit and every dollar is masked to those cells at the end of the calculation.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation and Tourism
text:
Quantity
Annual visits. For each Chebyshev ring at 1, 2, 3 and 4 grid cells, visit_potential_array turns a population cell into weekly visits through the gravity form
\[
v = \frac{1 + k}{k + e^{-\alpha P}}
\]
with a \(k\) and an \(\alpha\) per ring, and multiplies by 52 weeks. create_distance_kernel builds the ring, the full 3 by 3 block for ring 1 and the cells exactly \(n\) steps away for larger rings, and pygeoprocessing.convolve_2d spreads each cell’s potential over its ring. The rings accumulate into one visit total per cell.
The population raster is residents for daily recreation. For tourism it is allocate_overnights_raster, which spreads each country’s UNWTO overnight total proportionally over that country’s hotel pixels. read_unwto_sheets in the task module locates each sheet’s data by its AFGHANISTAN header row, and clean_unwto_data builds the overnight panel from the domestic and inbound accommodation sheets, preferring the Total row over Hotels-and-similar where Total exists. build_country_overnights_map sums domestic and international overnights per country at the target year.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation and Tourism
text:
Price
The national fuel cost per kilometre, column gasoline_cost_usd_per_km_2019_gppdata, multiplied by the ring distance. value_potential_array computes the ring distance as buffer_zone * pixel_size and charges ring_distance - 0.5 * pixel_size.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation and Tourism
text:
Valuation
value_potential_array multiplies annual visits by that travel cost, ring by ring, and the rings accumulate the same way the visits do. sum_rasters_by_country_id then sums the four result rasters over the country-id raster, and gep_calculation sets
\[
\text{recreation GEP} = \text{daily value} + \text{tourist value}
\]
Aggregation happens directly on r250, because the source pipeline’s own country-id raster is iso3_r250_id. The aggregation surface and the one-row-per-country collapse coincide, so no r264 sum can double-count here.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation and Tourism
text:
Inputs
From es_config.csv, gep_regions_input_path is cartographic/ee/ee_r250.gpkg and gep_regions_id_col is iso3_r250_id.
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the recreation service:

recreation_lulc_share_path_template, the per-class 1 km share rasters, formatted with each land-cover class.
recreation_pa_share_path, the accessible protected-area share.
recreation_road_distance_path, the distance-to-road raster.
recreation_road_length_path, used only as the 1 km reference grid for rasterisation.
recreation_population_path, the WorldPop residents raster.
recreation_fuel_cost_path, the per-country fuel cost table.
recreation_unwto_path, the UNWTO all-data workbook.
recreation_hotels_path, the hotel point layer.

File names are kept exactly as the drive ships them, including the fuel-cost CSV’s spelling, so staging is a copy rather than a rename layer.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation and Tourism
text:
Outputs
Each task writes into its own directory: env_index_1km.tif, accessibility_index_1km.tif, rec_sites_ranked_1km.tif and high_quality_sites_1km.tif, then iso3_r250_ids_1km.tif, hotels_1km.tif, unwto_panel.csv and overnights_1km.tif, then site_visits_1km.tif and site_value_1km.tif for the daily and tourist channels.
gep_calculation writes gep_by_country_base_year.csv, holding the r250 identifiers and attributes, year, daily_visits, daily_value, tourist_visits, tourist_value and recreation_gep. A companion .gpkg expands the same values across r264 sub-regions for mapping only, never summed.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation and Tourism
text:
Compute
sum_rasters_by_country_id aggregates whole arrays, which is the source repository’s approach and is kept for anchor fidelity. At 1 km global that holds several arrays of roughly 4 GB at once, so run it on a machine with headroom.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation and Tourism
text:
What is open
A units question is flagged and deliberately not fixed. The travel-cost distance is buffer_zone * pixel_size with pixel_size read from the raster, which is degrees on a 4326 grid, while the fuel-cost column is USD per kilometre. The port is faithful to the source. Resolve it against the reference results_by_country.csv once the data and the anchor are staged, then fix the code and this document together.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text: Air filtration is valued as avoided mortality. Vegetation captures dry pollutants, fewer people die, and those deaths are priced at a value of statistical life. One workbook on the consortium drive carries two channels, so this module writes two service columns. Deposition is the air filtration service. Dust, meaning windblown-dust suppression, is the sandstorm prevention service, which has its own row on the account sheet and no module of its own. The base year is 2019 and the price convention recorded in es_config.csv is VSL (avoided mortality).

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Quantity
Avoided deaths per country per channel, the workbook’s Dep_Deaths and Dust_Deaths columns.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Price
The workbook’s VSL column. Where a country has its own VSL the workbook marks VSL_Source as country. Where it does not, the row is marked global_avg and carries the mean of the country-source VSLs. verify_global_average_fill asserts that rule at rtol 1e-9 and raises if the workbook stops following it.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Valuation
air_quality_benefits recomputes both products from the workbook’s own columns:
\[\text{air filtration GEP} = \text{Dep\_Deaths} \times \text{VSL}, \qquad
\text{sandstorm prevention GEP} = \text{Dust\_Deaths} \times \text{VSL}\]
The tests hold that recomputation to the workbook’s own benefit columns. The deposition total, $17.81bn, is the manuscript’s air-filtration number.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Joining to countries
air_quality_gep_by_country joins the workbook onto the r250 ids by position, because both the workbook and the reference order are the r250 geopackage in row order and the workbook’s FID is the geopackage feature id. The join refuses to proceed unless the row counts match and at least AIR_FILTRATION_MIN_NAME_MATCHES names are identical. 199 of 250 names are identical, and the rest differ only in sovereign versus territory naming of the same rows.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the air_filtration service:

air_filtration_workbook_path, the committed per-country workbook, with a _source_note row recording that it comes from the drive’s air filtration folder rather than a public URL.

reference/r250_gpkg_order.csv ships inside the module and supplies the row order the positional join checks against.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Output
gep_calculation writes gep_by_country_base_year.csv into its own task directory, holding the r250 identifiers and attributes, year, air_filtration_gep and sandstorm_prevention_gep. Both totals are logged.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Method constants

AIR_FILTRATION_VSL_USA = 9_900_000, the US anchor VSL the documented method starts from.
AIR_FILTRATION_MIN_NAME_MATCHES = 190, the sanity floor under the positional join.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Taken as given
The science behind the avoided-death columns, a coupled set of process-based emissions models, Global InMAP and health impacts as the appendix describes it, is not rebuildable here and is adopted as published. The valuation layer on top of it is rebuilt and verified against the workbook exactly.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
What is open
The VSL build behind the workbook. The folder’s vsl.R and its raw CSVs document a US-anchored, GDP- and life-years-adjusted method, and gdp_adjusted_vsl ports that method for transparency, scaling the US VSL per life-year lost by GDP and applying it to each country’s own life expectancy minus median age. Run against the committed raw data it does not reproduce the workbook’s VSL column, which points to a different data vintage. That vintage gap is a named ask.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text: Extractive materials provision covers mineral extraction. The account values it from two World Bank series, the share of a country’s GDP that mineral rents represent and the GDP itself, with an attribution factor applied to the resulting rent. The base year is 2019.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Quantity
GDP in current USD, the World Bank series NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, read from the path recorded in es_config.csv as gep_quantity_input_path.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Price
Mineral rents as a percentage of GDP, the World Bank series NY.GDP.MINR.RT.ZS, read from the path recorded in es_config.csv as gep_attribution_input_path.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Attribution
A factor of 0.49 is applied to the rent. MINERAL_RENT_GEP_FACTOR holds it in the tasks module.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Valuation
mineral_rent_gep is the whole product:
\[
\text{GEP} = \frac{\text{mineral rent (\% of GDP)}}{100} \times \text{GDP (current USD)} \times 0.49
\]
The task reads each wide World Bank CSV and passes the frame to world_bank_wide_to_long, which melts the year columns into long form keyed on Country Code and drops the descriptive columns by not naming them. The two long tables are merged on Country Code and year and deduplicated on that pair. collapse_countries_to_r250 reduces the r264 correspondence to one canonical row per country before the join, so a country that r264 splits is not repeated. The base-year table is the rows where year equals p.gep_base_year. group_countries aggregates the value column by year for the time series.
Country references are published at 30 arcsecond simplification for this service, rather than the 300 arcsecond default the other modules use.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Inputs
Both data paths come from es_config.csv rather than es_parameters.csv. The extractive_materials_provision row names gep_quantity_input_path for the GDP series and gep_attribution_input_path for the mineral rent share, along with gep_regions_input_path as cartographic/ee/ee_r264_correspondence.gpkg and gep_regions_id_col as ee_r264_id. The service has no es_parameters.csv rows.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Outputs
gep_calculation writes four tables into its own task directory:

gep_by_country_year_mineral.csv, the merged long table with the valuation column.
gep_by_country_year.csv, the same table carried forward.
gep_by_country_base_year.csv, the 2019 rows, plus a matching .gpkg for mapping.
gep_by_year.csv and an .xlsx alongside it, the annual totals.

The valuation column is extractive_materials_provision_gep, mirrored into a Value column for the annual aggregation.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Method constants
MINERAL_RENT_GEP_FACTOR = 0.49, applied to mineral rents times GDP in the valuation.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Taken as given
Both World Bank series are used as published.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
What is open
The attribution factor’s provenance is undocumented as of 2026-08-16. There is no source for 0.49 in the code, in the drive submission, or in its raw_data notes, and it is an open question for the service owner. The staged reference output embeds the factor, so it should not change without an owner-blessed source.
gep_by_country_year.csv and gep_by_country_year_mineral.csv are the same table written twice. The valuation produces one row per country and year, so there is nothing for the second table to add until the service gains a per-mineral breakdown.

title: Coastal blue carbon
text: Value the carbon held in the world’s three mapped coastal blue-carbon habitats (mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass) as part of Gross Ecosystem Product. The quantity is mapped habitat area multiplied by a per-habitat carbon density; the price is the same annual rental social cost of carbon that terrestrial carbon storage is valued at (Parisa et al. 2022). The service values storage only. The figure it reports is the carbon standing in the base year, not a flow between years.

title: Coastal blue carbon
text: Value the carbon held in the world’s three mapped coastal blue-carbon habitats (mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass) as part of Gross Ecosystem Product. The quantity is mapped habitat area multiplied by a per-habitat carbon density; the price is the same annual rental social cost of carbon that terrestrial carbon storage is valued at (Parisa et al. 2022). The service values storage only. The figure it reports is the carbon standing in the base year, not a flow between years.

title: Coastal blue carbon
text:
Method

Extent
Each habitat comes from its own published extent map, read as polygons:







Habitat
Extent




Mangrove
Global Mangrove Watch v3, 2019 (Bunting et al. 2018, 2022)


Salt marsh
GLC_FCS30D 2019, a 30 m land-cover product; the marsh class extracted to global_salt_marsh2019.gpkg (Zhang et al. 2024)


Seagrass
UNEP-WCMC013-014 SeagrassPtPy v7.1 (UNEP-WCMC and Short 2021)



Seagrass is optional at the tree level (include_seagrass). A tree built with seagrass but no extent file raises rather than running, so a data gap cannot quietly understate the coastal total; a tree built without seagrass writes every seagrass column at zero, so the combined table has the same shape either way.


Aggregation surface
Coastal habitat is aggregated on the marine surface, eemarine_r566 (one row per exclusive economic zone and coastal region) rather than on the land country surface the other services use. Each habitat layer is clipped to every marine region in turn, and the clipped pieces are measured in the equal-area projection EPSG:6933 (NSIDC EASE-Grid 2.0 Global), which is what turns polygon geometry into hectares.
Salt marsh additionally runs a zonal pass over the hectares-per-cell pyramid, written out as salt_marsh_with_area.gpkg for inspection. The area that reaches the country table is the equal-area geometric area, the same measure the other two habitats use.


Carbon density
Density is resolved per pixel for mangrove and salt marsh, and per polygon for seagrass. Every pool is reported in Mg C per hectare, and soil carbon throughout is the stock in the top 20 cm. The external soil products report the top 1 m, and are taken as a linear share of that profile.
Mangrove. Above-ground biomass follows the Hamilton & Friess latitude regression (Hamilton and Friess 2018), AGB (t/ha) = −6.4305 × |lat| + 271.747, floored at zero (the line crosses zero at roughly 42°, and the floor is what stops it going negative beyond that). Below-ground biomass is AGB times the IPCC zone-specific root-to-shoot ratio (IPCC 2014): 0.49 in the wet tropics, 0.29 in the dry tropics, 0.96 subtropical, with the tropical boundary at |lat| = 23.5° and the wet/dry split at 2000 mm mean annual precipitation. Biomass converts to carbon at 0.48 for AGB (Hamilton and Friess 2018) and 0.39 for BGB (Howard et al. 2014). Soil carbon is read from the Sanderman 30 m mangrove soil map (Sanderman et al. 2018). Where no precipitation raster is supplied the whole tropics take the wet ratio; where no soil raster is supplied, soil falls back to a latitude step function running from 80 Mg C/ha at the equator down to 50 Mg C/ha poleward of 25°.
Salt marsh. Above-ground biomass is the Chmura median of 5 t/ha (Chmura et al. 2003), raised by a factor of 1.2 below |lat| = 25° for tropical productivity. Below-ground biomass is 2.5 times AGB, for the extensive root systems of tidal marsh. Carbon fractions are 0.45 for AGB and 0.41 for BGB. Soil carbon is read from the Maxwell MarSOC map of tidal marsh soils (Maxwell et al. 2024); the fallback step function runs the other way from mangrove, 36 Mg C/ha in the tropics up to 70 Mg C/ha poleward of 45°.
Seagrass. Biomass carbon is genus-specific, from the Gomis global synthesis (Gomis et al. 2025), and is the one density that is an attribute of the polygon rather than of the pixel, the extent map carries a GENUS field. Genera group by life-history strategy: persistent (Posidonia at 9.78 Mg C/ha, the other persistent genera at 3.70), opportunistic (Zostera, Syringodium, Halodule at 0.94) and colonising (Ruppia 0.33, Halophila 0.19). A polygon whose genus is unknown, unreported or absent from the table takes the global mean, 1.55 Mg C/ha. Biomass splits 30% above ground and 70% below. Soil carbon is a constant 22 Mg C/ha, the Fourqurean global mean for the top 20 cm (Fourqurean et al. 2012). Freshwater genera present in the extent map (Trapa, Myriophyllum, Valisneria, Najas and the rest) are zeroed across every pool, soil included, so they contribute nothing to a country’s stock.


Stock
For mangrove and salt marsh, stock is accumulated pixel by pixel on the 10 arc-second grid. Each pixel’s density is evaluated at its latitude, multiplied by the hectares in that cell, and added to the marine region it falls in. A pixel counts only where the habitat mask is set, a region id is present and the cell has area. A no-data pixel inside a soil raster contributes zero soil rather than a missing value, and its biomass still counts. The pass runs in row blocks and skips any block the habitat does not reach.
For seagrass, stock is each clipped polygon’s genus density multiplied by its hectares, summed to the region.
Every habitat therefore reports four columns per region: above-ground, below-ground and soil carbon, and their sum. The total is always the three pools added, never a separately computed figure, so it cannot drift away from the parts it is printed beside.


Price and valuation
The price is the annual rental social cost of carbon for the base year, read from the carbon price series (carbon_prices.xlsx) under the run’s price convention, the same series and convention terrestrial carbon uses, so the two carbon services are priced identically. GEP is then
\[
\text{GEP}_{\text{coastal carbon}} = \text{carbon stock (Mg C)} \times \text{rental SCC (\$ per Mg C)}
\]
applied pool by pool, so the written table carries a value for above-ground, below-ground and soil carbon as well as the habitat total. The year and the price used travel in the table beside the values.


Collapse to one row per country
The service produces two tables. The first, gep_by_country_base_year_r566, is the full marine surface: per-habitat area, stock pools and storage values for each of the r566 marine regions, with a matching GeoPackage for mapping. Regions with no coastal habitat at all are dropped from it, they are ocean rows, not zero-value countries.
The second, gep_by_country_base_year, is the country table. Building it takes two steps that each guard against counting the same coast twice:

Keep the _EEZ rows. The marine surface carries a country’s coast more than once, as an EEZ row plus land and territorial rows over the same habitat. Only the _EEZ rows are valued.
Collapse through the canonical r264 row. The r264 correspondence splits large countries into sub-regions (China ×6, India ×6, and four two-way splits), so it is filtered to ee_r264_label == iso3_r250_label before the join. Without that filter the join repeats a split country once per sub-region and the sum multiplies its value. Countries with no coastal habitat report zero rather than dropping out.

title: Coastal blue carbon
section: Open question: EEZ-only versus all rows
text:
Open question: EEZ-only versus all rows
Step 1 above is a choice, not a cleanup. Valuing every r566 row instead of the _EEZ rows returns a strictly larger total, and the gap is exactly the non-EEZ rows, the same coastal habitat counted again under a land or territorial label. The two totals answer different questions. What the module writes is the EEZ-only figure; the all-rows figure is what summing the r566 table gives, and the module does not compute it. The arithmetic of the distinction is pinned in test_eez_only_is_a_strict_subset_of_all_rows.

title: Coastal blue carbon
text:
Sensitivity worth naming
The latitude fallbacks, mangrove soil without the Sanderman raster, salt marsh soil without MarSOC, and the mangrove root ratio without a precipitation raster, change the number a run produces. Which source each run used is written to the log at the point the raster is aligned.

title: Coastal blue carbon
text:
Outputs
Per habitat, in the habitat’s own task directory:

<habitat>_area_by_countries2019.{gpkg,csv} (hectares per marine region.
<habitat>_carbon_stock_by_countries2019.csv) the four stock pools per marine region (Mg C).
<habitat>_storage_value_by_countries2019.csv, the stock pools priced (USD), with the year and the rental SCC used.

Then, across habitats:

combined_ecosystem_areas.csv, every habitat’s area and stock on one row per marine region, plus total coastal area and total carbon stock.
gep_by_country_base_year_r566.{csv,gpkg} (the marine-surface GEP detail.
gep_by_country_base_year.csv) one row per country, the service’s GEP result.

title: GTAPpy development notes
text:
NoteHistorical record, not a guide



These are dated notes from the 2022–2023 build-out of GTAPpy, kept because they record why several conventions are the way they are and what was still open at the time. The code shown has since moved to the run_project(p) run-file convention described in Conventions, so do not copy from it. For current usage start at GTAPpy.




The open question this entry records: how to get from an Erwin-style mapping workbook to the EE spec correspondence format.
This is what a region correspondence looks like as it arrives:



GTAP-ctry2reg as downloaded, before conversion


Two problems with it as a machine-readable input. First, the file has to be renamed to say what it actually maps — gtapv7_r251_r160_correspondence.xlsx (and it has to stay .xlsx rather than CSV, because the mapping spans multiple worksheets). Second, No. is used twice in the same sheet, once numbering the r160 regions and once the r251 ones. Any parser reading it positionally gets this wrong, so the input format needs to disambiguate the two.
Legend information is also carried inside the region correspondence sheet, which is the wrong home for it — it needs a deliberate place of its own rather than being attached to whichever correspondence happened to need it.
The same pattern applies to sectors, which is the converted, EE-spec shape:



The converted correspondence: regions, sectors, activities and commodities as parallel blocks


A terminology note worth preserving: “sector” is used here specifically for the case where you are not distinguishing COMM (commodities) from ACTS (activities) — at the time these notes were written the distinction had not been pinned down.



Proposals raised against the model release layout, and how they resolved.
Naming.

In the release’s Data folder, the aggregation label gtapaez11-50 should be v11-s26-r50 — database version, sector count, region count.
The most recent release carries no timestamp; dated versions of a same-named model or aggregation take the timestamp of when they were first released.
CMF files renamed from cwon_bau.cmf to gtapv7-aez-rd_bau.cmf, and cwon_bau-es.cmf to gtapv7-aez-rd_bau-es.cmf — hyphens join parts of one variable, underscores split the name into its list of fields.
SIMRUN becomes just the experiment name (bau) rather than project name plus experiment.

Project structure.

Drop set PROJ=cwon from the CMF — the project is defined by the ProjectFlow object, not the command file.
Separate data and output from the code release:
set MODd=..\mod      set CMFd=.\cmf
set SOLd=..\out      set DATd=..\data%AGG%
SOLd and DATd deliberately live outside the release.
The goal is that a release can be run either by calling the batch file or by calling the Python run script, so the two are kept as close as possible. The asymmetry is intentional and one-directional: the batch file can only reproduce a resource-depletion run without ecosystem services, so the Python script can wrap the batch file but not the reverse.
CMF command-line options renamed to match what they are: gtap_base_data_dir, starting_data_file_path, output_dir, starting_year, ending_year (previously positional p1–p5). experiment_label may not be renameable, as it appears to be fixed by the CMF filename.

Answers from Erwin.

Can the raw GEMPACK output be read to estimate progress, for a progress bar? Yes, when running with automatic accuracy — GEMPACK reports its position:
+++> Beginning subinterval number 4.
---> Beginning pass number 1 of 2-pass calculation, subinterval 4.
Beginning pass number 6 of 6-pass calculation, subinterval 6
Could years drop the Y prefix (Y2018), which breaks string→int conversion? No — keep the Y. GEMPACK variable names cannot begin with a non-numeric… that is, cannot begin with a numeral.
There is no bau-SUM_Y2050, though there is for VOL and WEL — is that intentional? No: SUM describes the starting database, so a terminal-year SUM is meaningless. Relatedly, welfare cannot be produced in a resource-depletion run because there is no discount rate.
Is everything stored in the .sl4, making the other files redundant? No. Conversions such as results in volume terms are not in the .sl4 and have to come from sltoht or ViewSOL.




Shocks implemented at this point: population file replacement, GDP change, and (tentatively) yield changes.
The run file of the era created the ProjectFlow object at the top and added tasks to it — the ancestor of today’s task tree:



The 2022-era run file: ProjectFlow object, aggregation and experiment labels, tasks added explicitly


Note the shape already visible here: a list of aggregation labels ('10x10', '65x141') and a list of experiment labels ('agpr20b', 'beef50', 'rtms5'), iterated over as a cross product. That is the multi-aggregation philosophy described on the GTAPpy home page, present from the start.
And the task that generated a CMF and called the executable:



run_gtap_v7_executable: per-aggregation, per-experiment CMF generation and invocation


The interesting part is the if not hb.path_exists(expected_sl4_path) guard — skip-if-already-computed, done by hand before it was pushed down into ProjectFlow — and the per-aggregation override of xSets, xSubsets and Shock, since the 10×10 aggregation needs different set members than the 141×65 default.
What was hard. The open problem at this date was making shocks work generally: producing xSets, xSubsets and Shock statements per scenario, with READFROMFILE in the TABLO CMF as the mechanism for file-driven values. The taxonomy that came out of it is on Running GTAP by hand.
A distinction from this entry worth restating, because it caused confusion: there are shocks and there are data updates, and replacing an elasticity file is the latter. If you swap in basedata2 with a matching default2.prm and apply no shock, the model reproduces that database — the elasticities are, in that sense, calibrated to it. A supply-response elasticity behaves differently and will move the results.
Population shocks needed one more preprocessing step: the value has to be a percentage change over the default POP in the base data, so an external population file is read in and processed against the base rather than used directly.

title: Run templates
text:
The examples/ directory of the devstack repository exists to answer one question: what should my run file look like? A run file is the single script that builds a ProjectFlow, defines a task tree, and executes it — the file a collaborator opens first and the file you copy when you start a project.
The directory holds four kinds of material:

title: Run templates
text:
Where the files are
The templates are Python files in the devstack repository, not on this site. Browse or copy them here:

examples/run_templates/ — the copy-me set
examples/run_templates_annotated/ — the same code with the reasoning written out
examples/input_research_scripts/ — real run files and the raw scripts they replace

Clone the repo, or copy a single file straight out of GitHub.

title: Run templates
text:
Start here
The four numbered templates run with nothing downloaded — each generates its own synthetic arrays — so you can execute all of them before touching base data. (run_template_seals_example.py in the same directory is the exception: it drives a real model. See the note under the rung table.)
conda activate env1
cd earth_economy_devstack/examples/run_templates
python run_template_1_minimal.py
Then run it a second time. It finishes almost instantly: every task is behind an existence check, so ProjectFlow skips what it already computed. That skip-if- already-computed behavior, one output folder per task, and logging are the whole payoff of the ~25 lines in template 1.
Outputs do not land in the repo. Because the script lives inside a cloned repo, bare hb.ProjectFlow() places the project directory just outside it, at <repo_parent>/projects/<name derived from the filename> — the stem minus the run_ prefix, so run_template_1_minimal.py writes to Files/projects/template_1_minimal/. Look inside: input/, intermediate/, output/, and a folder per task.

title: Run templates
section: Three axes, and the one that is numbered
text:
Three axes, and the one that is numbered
A run file’s complexity is three independent questions, and a project sits somewhere on each:

Configuration — how a run varies. Levels 1–4, the four templates below.
Code layout — where the code lives: single file → split (<project>_tasks.py, _functions.py, _utils.py, _initialize_project.py) → library package.
Ownership — who owns the code you run: self-contained → devstack developer → downstream user, where the library is a read-only dependency in your own repo.

Only configuration is numbered, because only configuration is a ladder climbed in order. The axes are independent — global_invest’s service runners are configuration level 2 with a library-package layout. Every template’s docstring states its position on all three. The full model is in project_complexity.qmd.

title: Run templates
text:
The four configuration levels
Templates 1–4 hold code layout and ownership fixed (single file, self-contained), so configuration is the only thing changing between them — that is what makes them readable as a diff. Read them in order. Each adds exactly one mechanism, and each docstring says when to move up — the point is to earn complexity rather than adopt it.



#
file
adds
promote when




1
run_template_1_minimal.py
one task function, p.add_task(), p.execute()
you add a second task


2
run_template_2_script_with_tree.py
build_task_tree(p); several tasks that chain by publishing paths; constants inline in __main__
you want a second variant of the run


3
run_template_3_canonical.py
run_project(p) + a scenarios CSV; variants are data, not forked code
a machine-specific value tries to enter the code


4
run_template_4_data_driven.py
a parameters CSV, nested tasks via parent=, a cross-scenario report task
you need parallel iterators or more CSV classes



Alongside the four rungs, run_templates/run_template_seals_example.py is the same anatomy applied to a real model: build_task_tree delegates unchanged to seals_initialize_project.build_standard_task_tree(p), and run_project sets the base data dir and the processing resolution and loads the scenarios CSV, which ships in seals’ tracked input_template/ and is seeded into input/ on first run (runtime CSV generation was retired 2026-08; it returns typed as generate_scenarios_csv_from_model_spec). Copy this one to start a standalone SEALS project. It is the one template that moves along the other two axes while staying at configuration level 3: its code layout is a library package (nothing in the file defines a task) and its ownership is devstack developer (seals is imported, and you could edit it). Moving along code layout changed exactly one function — build_task_tree, which now delegates instead of containing. One practical difference from templates 3 and 4: it needs seals installed and will download base data on its first run, so it is not a five-second toy like the others. For ownership one step further — seals as a read-only dependency in your own repo — copy run_template_downstream_user.py instead.

title: Run templates
text:
The other two axes
Two further templates in run_templates/ hold configuration fixed at level 4 and move along one of the other axes each. Both compute exactly the same numbers as run_template_4_data_driven.py, which is the point — diff them against it and the only difference is the axis named.



file
axis it moves
what changes




run_template_split_layout.py
Code layout → split
tasks leave the run file for four siblings: caloric_yield_tasks.py, _functions.py, _utils.py, _initialize_project.py. Exactly one function in the run file changes — build_task_tree now delegates instead of containing.


run_template_downstream_user.py
Ownership → downstream user
imports caloric_yield_initialize_project as a read-only dependency, then adds its own task after the library builder returns. Note it is back to a single-file layout while being further along ownership — the axes really are independent.



The _utils / _functions split is the rule worth internalising: <project>_utils.py is science-unaware and therefore a promotion queue — when a second project needs one of those helpers, it belongs in hazelbean. <project>_functions.py encodes the model’s domain knowledge and is terminal. If nothing ever leaves your _utils, you are not applying the rule.
run_template_downstream_user.py also states the one thing the ownership axis has not solved: attaching a task to a specific library task (parent=p.yield_analysis_task) works only because builders assign p.<name>_task as a side effect, and no contract says which of those names are public API. Until one exists, attach at the top level and depend on published paths rather than on task objects.
Rung 3 is the canonical anatomy, and all four of its parts are required at that level:

build_task_tree(p) — what the pipeline is. Nothing but add_task calls.
run_project(p) — how it is executed. Returns p.
the __main__ guard — importing a run file must never start a run. It is also where this project’s own configuration lives.
a scenarios CSV — the rows of work.


The rule that runs through rungs 3 and 4

run_project(p) sets what no variant ever changes. The caller sets what a variant might.

The caller builds the ProjectFlow and hangs configuration on it; run_project only runs it. When a constant starts varying, it moves one line up — out of run_project, into the caller. There is no signature to edit, no keyword to add, and no default that can drift out of sync. One deliberate exception (2026-08 amendment): the full definitions-filename block (parameters, scenarios, outputs, figures, sections, descriptions) is set by the caller even though most members never vary — it is the project’s interface manifest, and variants copy the block and override only the member that differs. Template 4 shows it working: the block sits in __main__, and run_project only loads it via hb.initialize_parameters / hb.initialize_scenarios. The split, downstream and seals templates additionally end their init with the model’s initialize_project(p) — the model-initializer anatomy.
The cost, stated honestly: bare run_project() no longer works — the caller must hand it a ProjectFlow, and a variant wrapper is four lines instead of three. In exchange every knob a run uses is visible at the call site, and forgetting one raises a named AttributeError instead of silently using somebody else’s default.


A variant run is its own file, never a fork
This is the habit the ladder exists to build. run_templates_annotated/run_template_3_canonical_test.py is the whole answer to the “copy the run file and change one line” instinct:
import hazelbean as hb
from run_template_3_canonical import run_project

if __name__ == '__main__':
    p = hb.ProjectFlow(project_name='..._test', run_mode='check')
    p.scenario_definitions_filename = 'template_3_scenarios_test.csv'
    # p.tasks_to_skip = ['yield_summations']
    run_project(p)
It imports the pipeline unchanged. What differs is data (a one-row CSV) and placement (its own project dir) — never code. Both sets carry this file, because a wrapper is something you copy: run_templates/run_template_3_canonical_test.py is the one to start from.


run_mode
Templates 3 and 4 pass run_mode to the constructor:

'check' — reuse the stable project dir; recompute only what is missing. The default working mode.
'fresh_intermediate' — redo all computation but keep input/. Test projects only.
'full' — a fresh, timestamped project dir; everything re-runs.



input_template/ and the machine-specific values
Both template sets keep their CSVs in a tracked input_template/ directory next to the run file. On first run ProjectFlow copies anything missing into the project’s untracked input/ and never overwrites the working copy. That is why template_4_parameters.csv ships with data_credentials_path blank: you fill it in your machine’s input/ copy, and it never reaches the code or git.







CSV
what it is




template_3_scenarios.csv
four scenario rows (scenario_label, yield_offset, year)


template_3_scenarios_test.csv
the same schema, one row — the variant run


template_4_scenarios.csv
scenarios for template 4


template_4_parameters.csv
key,value constants: ndv, n_rows, n_cols, and blank data_credentials_path



The three-column scenarios CSV in these templates is illustrative only. The real schema is specified in proposed_changes.qmd; worked instances of it are in scenario_definitions_examples/.

title: Run templates
text:
The two template sets
run_templates/ and run_templates_annotated/ are the same four rungs computing the same toy project (sum caloric yield across scenarios). They differ only in how much they say:

run_templates/ — concise. Comments only where a line is non-obvious. This is the set to copy into a new project.
run_templates_annotated/ — the same code with long docstrings covering what each level is for, what it deliberately does not have, why the conventions are what they are, and when to move along an axis. Read these once; copy from the other directory.

run_templates/ additionally holds run_template_split_layout.py and run_template_downstream_user.py (the other two axes) with their caloric_yield_* modules; the annotated set covers the configuration axis only. The input_template/ CSVs are otherwise identical between the sets.
Templates 1 and 2 use bare hb.ProjectFlow() in both sets, so they share a project directory across the sets — harmless, since they compute the same thing. Templates 3 and 4 carry distinct project names and get their own directories.

title: Run templates
text:
input_research_scripts/
Real scripts collected as source material: the input to conversion work, and the reference implementations that conversion produces. Read these; copy from run_templates/. Three groups:
Reference implementations — the conventions at full scale:

run_invest_carbon_in_projectflow.py — the run_project(p) convention on the global_invest InVEST carbon task tree. The variant knob is p.aoi (an ISO3 code or 'global'); paths resolve through p.get_path(), which searches the project input dir, then base data, then the cloud.
ngfs_pnas.py — the largest reference implementation of the canonical anatomy: a two-pass GTAP+SEALS pipeline whose build_task_tree is driven by a shock_config column in the scenarios CSV. It shows the anatomy holding at a scale where the task tree runs to hundreds of lines: run_project(p) is still nothing but constants, and every knob a run varies is still visible in the __main__ guard.
ngfs_pnas_test.py — its pared test run: same task tree, a minimal scenarios CSV, one policy scenario, one year, one region. The variant-is-a-file habit at full scale.
seals_standard.py — a standard SEALS run, identical to run_templates/run_template_seals_example.py.

Converted, but not exemplary — useful for what they get wrong:

yanxu_carbon.py, cc_carbon.py — GEP carbon runs on ProjectFlow, with hardcoded absolute base_data_dir paths pointing at somebody else’s machine. cc_carbon.py also has no __main__ guard, so importing it starts a run.

Not on ProjectFlow at all — the before-pictures:

research_script.py — a working pollination analysis with hardcoded D:\Shared drives\... paths throughout. The canonical example of a script that cannot run on any other machine.
research_script_relative_paths.py — the same script after one improvement: paths built from a single base_data_dir. Still not a ProjectFlow run file; a useful intermediate step.
invest_carbon_script.py — an InVEST-generated standalone script, the form the InVEST UI exports. Compare with run_invest_carbon_in_projectflow.py to see what wrapping it in a task tree buys.

title: Run templates
text:
Data examples
scenario_definitions_examples/ holds instances of the v2 scenario definitions schema specified in proposed_changes.qmd:

single_stage_seals.csv — a SEALS-only project, including a hindcast year.
multi_stage_ngfs.csv — GTAP + SEALS: a 2020-anchored canonical clock with a gtap stage clock.
hindcast_example.csv — a minimal demonstration of backward years.

title: Run templates
text:
Where to go next

project_complexity.qmd — the ladder from a one-off script to a systematic project, and why each rung is earned.
project_flow.qmd — the ProjectFlow engine itself: tasks, iterators, project dirs, get_path.
conventions.qmd — the full EE Spec naming and structure rules.
proposed_changes.qmd — the scenarios CSV schema.

title: The stages of project complexity
text:
The short answer: research code fails at the seams between runs, not inside them. A script that computes the right number once is easy. What is hard is everything that happens afterwards — running it again with one input changed, running it four hundred times over scenarios, running it on someone else’s machine, running it on data too large to hold in memory, and still being able to say two years later exactly which code and which inputs produced figure 3.
Almost every research codebase answers those by copying: copy the script and edit one line, copy the block and change the index, comment out the slow part with a boolean. That works until it doesn’t, and when it stops working it does so silently — a stale intermediate file, a copied block where one index was never updated, a hardcoded path that meant something different on the machine the results came from.
The devstack’s answer is a single move applied over and over: make the thing that varies data rather than code. Scenarios become rows in a CSV instead of copied blocks. Machine-specific values become a parameters CSV instead of hardcoded paths. What has already been computed becomes files on disk instead of a commented-out boolean, so a re-run skips it automatically. What runs, and in what order, becomes a task tree instead of top-to-bottom statements — which is also what lets independent branches run in parallel. Hazelbean, and ProjectFlow inside it, are the machinery that makes that move cheap enough to be the default.
None of this is adopted up front. Each piece exists because a specific pain demanded it, and the rest of this page is that history: the questions that got progressively harder, and the tool each one forced. If your problem is still a one-script problem, the honest advice is to write the one script — the point of the stages is to let you recognize the moment you have outgrown it.



As an introduction and/or motivation for using the software in the EE Devstack, I would like to talk through the process that I went through as a PhD student, postdoc and staff researcher to answer progressively harder questions. I break these out into 6 stages below. Solving these challenges is what led to the creation of Hazelbean and many other software solutions.



Here is an example script that you might write as an Earth-economy researcher. Suppose your adviser asks you “what is the total caloric yield on earth per hectare?” You might write a script like this:
import os
import numpy as np
import gdal

yield_per_hectare_raster_path = os.path.join('data', 'yield_per_cell.tif')
yield_per_hectare_raster = gdal.Open(yield_per_hectare_raster_path)
yield_per_hectare_array = yield_per_hectare_raster.ReadAsArray()

sum_of_yield = np.sum(yield_per_hectare_array)

print('The total caloric yield on earth per hectare is: ' + str(sum_of_yield))



This is where most research code goes to die, in my experience. Suppose your advisor now asks okay do this for the a bunch of different datasets on yield. The classic coder response is to make a longer script!
import os
import numpy as np
import gdal

yield_per_hectare_raster_path_1 = os.path.join('data', 'yield_per_cell_1.tif')
yield_per_hectare_raster_1 = gdal.Open(yield_per_hectare_raster_path_1)
yield_per_hectare_array_1 = yield_per_hectare_raster_1.ReadAsArray()

sum_of_yield_1 = np.sum(yield_per_hectare_array_1)

print('The total caloric yield on earth per hectare for dataset 1 is: ' + str(sum_of_yield_1))

yield_per_hectare_raster_path_2 = os.path.join('data', 'yield_per_cell_2.tif')
yield_per_hectare_raster_2 = gdal.Open(yield_per_hectare_raster_path_2)
yield_per_hectare_array_2 = yield_per_hectare_raster_2.ReadAsArray()

sum_of_yield_2 = np.sum(yield_per_hectare_array_2)

print('The total caloric yield on earth per hectare for dataset 2 is: ' + str(sum_of_yield_2))

yield_per_hectare_raster_path_3 = os.path.join('data', 'yield_per_cell_3.tif')
yield_per_hectare_raster_3 = gdal.Open(yield_per_hectare_raster_path_3)
yield_per_hectare_array_3 = yield_per_hectare_raster_3.ReadAsArray()

sum_of_yield_3 = np.sum(yield_per_hectare_array_2)

print('The total caloric yield on earth per hectare for dataset 3 is: ' + str(sum_of_yield_3))

yield_per_hectare_raster_path_4 = os.path.join('data', 'yield_per_cell_4.tif')
yield_per_hectare_raster_4 = gdal.Open(yield_per_hectare_raster_path_4)
yield_per_hectare_array_4 = yield_per_hectare_raster_4.ReadAsArray()

sum_of_yield_4 = np.sum(yield_per_hectare_array_4)

print('The total caloric yield on earth per hectare for dataset 4 is: ' + str(sum_of_yield_4))
This style of coding works, but will quickly cause you to lose your sanity. Who can find the reason the above code will cause your article to be retracted? Also, what if each of those summations takes a long time and you want to make a small change? You have to rerun the whole thing. This is bad.



The coding approach in stage 2 becomes intractable when there are lots of layers to consider. The final level of complexity we will discuss (before just using the Earth Economy Devstack approach) arises when the number of files that must be managed becomes a challenge both for performance reasons and the challenges of managing complexity.
One example where this comes up is when a computation requires writing tiles of output. In many big-data applications and in most of the very large datasets that are available online, the data are themselves stored in tiles. On the one hand, this is nice because it automatically suggests a chunk-by-chunk parallelization strategy. On the other hand, it quickly becomes challenging when, for instance, you want to look at an area of interest (AOI) that spans multiple tiles. There are a plethora of software solutions to deal with this, such as GDAL’s Virtual Raster (VRT) file type, but many of these have limitations.
When the computation in question requires many complex steps which might be contingent on other intermediate products from adjacent tiles, even some of the most cutting-edge solutions that implement complex tiling architecture (like DASK with rioxarray) will not be sufficient. This was the challenge that arose when doing downscaling with the SEALS model, especially when the algorithm had to be trained on such tiles millions of times. The optimized algorithm in this complex data and computation dependency-tree situation required a new tool, which would also have to address all of the above challenges in project complexity.
This led to ProjectFlow, one of the key tools within the Earth Economy Devstack and a part of Hazelbean.

title: The stages of project complexity
text:
The short answer: research code fails at the seams between runs, not inside them. A script that computes the right number once is easy. What is hard is everything that happens afterwards — running it again with one input changed, running it four hundred times over scenarios, running it on someone else’s machine, running it on data too large to hold in memory, and still being able to say two years later exactly which code and which inputs produced figure 3.
Almost every research codebase answers those by copying: copy the script and edit one line, copy the block and change the index, comment out the slow part with a boolean. That works until it doesn’t, and when it stops working it does so silently — a stale intermediate file, a copied block where one index was never updated, a hardcoded path that meant something different on the machine the results came from.
The devstack’s answer is a single move applied over and over: make the thing that varies data rather than code. Scenarios become rows in a CSV instead of copied blocks. Machine-specific values become a parameters CSV instead of hardcoded paths. What has already been computed becomes files on disk instead of a commented-out boolean, so a re-run skips it automatically. What runs, and in what order, becomes a task tree instead of top-to-bottom statements — which is also what lets independent branches run in parallel. Hazelbean, and ProjectFlow inside it, are the machinery that makes that move cheap enough to be the default.
None of this is adopted up front. Each piece exists because a specific pain demanded it, and the rest of this page is that history: the questions that got progressively harder, and the tool each one forced. If your problem is still a one-script problem, the honest advice is to write the one script — the point of the stages is to let you recognize the moment you have outgrown it.

title: The stages of project complexity
text: As an introduction and/or motivation for using the software in the EE Devstack, I would like to talk through the process that I went through as a PhD student, postdoc and staff researcher to answer progressively harder questions. title: The stages of project complexity
section: Where to start: earning complexity rather than adopting it
text:
Where to start: earning complexity rather than adopting it
Every template below is described on the Run Templates page, which is the place to start if you want to copy one.
Each tool in the six stages was adopted only when the previous stage’s pain demanded it — and that lesson applies to ProjectFlow itself. If your problem is still a stage-1 problem, do not start at configuration level 4. The spec scales down.
The smallest run file — a function becomes a task when you add it. The minimal ProjectFlow script is one task function plus a guarded three-line main block: p = hb.ProjectFlow(), p.add_task(your_function), p.execute(). Nothing is hidden — the add_task call is the moment a plain function becomes a task (and calling execute() with nothing added fails with a message telling you exactly that). See examples/run_templates/run_template_1_minimal.py — about 30 lines, and in exchange for roughly the effort of the stage-1 script you get an organized project directory, one folder per task, skip-if-already-computed re-runs, and logging.
The canonical form. When you want variants, graduate to configuration level 3: build_task_tree(p), run_project(p), and a __main__ guard that builds and configures the ProjectFlow. The rule that replaces a signature full of defaults: run_project(p) sets what no variant ever changes; the caller sets what a variant might. When a constant starts varying, it moves one line up, out of run_project and into the caller — no signature to edit and no default to keep in sync. (One deliberate exception, amended 2026-08: the caller sets the full definitions-filename block as the project’s interface manifest — see the conventions page.) See run_template_3_canonical.py, its annotated twin in examples/run_templates_annotated/ for the reasoning, and the conventions page for the full rules. For a project of your own that imports a devstack library as a read-only dependency, copy run_template_downstream_user.py into your repo as its run_<project>.py; for stock SEALS, copy run_seals.py. The full-scale reference implementation is ngfs_pnas (a private repository — ask for access).
When to move along an axis. Configuration: add a scenarios CSV when you first have two variants of the same run (the CSV, not the code, is what varies); add a parameters.csv key the first time a machine-specific value — an ssh host, a credentials path — tries to enter your code; add a thin run_<project>_test.py wrapper when the full run gets long enough to want a pared smoke test. Code layout: split when a task module gets big enough to navigate, or when a second run file needs the same task. Ownership: you cross into downstream-user territory the moment the library you import is one you should not be editing.
Every one of these is the stage-2 lesson in a new costume: the moment you are tempted to copy a block — or a whole file — and edit one line, the spec has a mechanism that varies the data instead of forking the code.

text:
Stage 1, redone with ProjectFlow

Old

import numpy as np
import gdal

New: P object organizes attributes
import os
import numpy as np
import gdal
import hazelbean as hb

# At this stage, p is honestly just a namespace — the code below works exactly as before.
# The payoff comes in the later stages, when everything already hanging off p gets you
# organized project directories, skip-if-already-computed re-runs, and auto-downloading
# data paths without restructuring your script. This line is the hook it all hangs on.
p = hb.ProjectFlow()

p.yield_per_hectare_raster_path = os.path.join('crops', 'yield_per_cell.tif') # Note for the future, we're defining a ref_path here but let's ignore that for now and assume it just goes in the p.input_dir
yield_per_hectare_raster = gdal.Open(p.yield_per_hectare_raster_path)
yield_per_hectare_array = yield_per_hectare_raster.ReadAsArray()

p.sum_of_yield = np.sum(yield_per_hectare_array)

print('The total caloric yield on earth per hectare is: ' + str(p.sum_of_yield))
One thing did already happen behind the scenes: hb.ProjectFlow() chose a sensible project directory for you. If your script lives inside a git repo (it probably does), ProjectFlow refuses to write outputs into the repo — it walks up to just outside it and uses <repo_parent>/projects/<name>, where <name> comes from your run file’s name. It logs the choice, and passing project_dir explicitly always overrides it. In the standard devstack layout this lands exactly where the full spec would put it, so nothing needs to change later as you climb the stages.
